speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to make a few additional remarks to those I was making the other night when time ran out. Quite frankly, I have lost count of the number of times I have spoken on this bill at its various stages. It has been a big disappointment to me that the government has not listened to the people directly affected by this metric bill. The people have spoken and the minister is aware of the feelings of the farmers of western Canada.
I need not spend time reading into the record the letters which I have received on this bill; to do so would take a good part of the day. As I have said in previous speeches, of all the letters I have received, I believe only one expressed any acceptance of the metric system, and even that was conditional acceptance. As I say, the minister is aware of the feelings of the people, not only from letters which he has received but also from the newspapers of western Canada. I am sure that he or the members of his staff have read those papers and will be aware that over the past few months the editorial pages have been filled with letters to the editor, 95 per cent of which oppose the metric system.
As usual, this government has adopted an arrogant and despotic attitude toward the people directly affected by this piece of legislation. The government seems to have adopted the attitude that it knows what is best for the people. I thought we were living in a democratic country, that 1 came to Ottawa to express the views of the people in my constituency, and that government members would be doing the same on behalf of the people in their constituencies. I thought they would be representing the views not only of their constituents but of the people of Canada at large. However, I found I was wrong.
Looking back over the record of this government, Mr. Speaker, I recall the capital punishment bill which was put through the House despite the fact that probably 80 per cent or 85 per cent, maybe more, of the people of Canada were opposed to the abolition of capital punishment. I also recall the gun control legislation which was finally dropped as a result of the official opposition taking a stand and carrying on a lengthy debate.
This metric bill is a civil service bill; it is a bureaucrat's piece of legislation. The minister and his colleagues in cabinet, as well as members on the government side, have been prepared to listen to the civil servants and not to the representations of the people affected by this bill. 1 recall being in committee when the bill was being discussed and we were listening to the evidence given by some of the civil servants who had been involved with this bill. They adopted an attitude, not of belligerency, but they suggested that those who were opposed to the bill were fools. I recall that when the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) closed the meeting one evening he gave quite a dissertation on what he thought of the attitude of the civil servants involved, and he said quite frankly, "If this was a private company and I was the manager, I would fire the lot of you".
During the committee stage of this bill and at report stage we gave the government the opportunity, by way of amendment, to alter the legislation in such a manner as to make it acceptable to the people of western Canada. I say "to the

people of western Canada" because they are the ones directly affected, although the effects of the Bill will ultimately be felt throughout the length and breadth of the country as changes begin to take place in our land measurement system. I think we will end up with a situation where, instead of having one method of land measurement, we will have three-acres, hectares and arpents. Eventually people in other parts of the country who at the moment are not directly affected by the bill will begin to realize the effects of the bill.
As I have said, we gave the government the opportunity, through amendments, to bring in a dual system, one that would be satisfactory to older farmers as well as to younger farmers who are more familiar with the metric system, so that ultimately we would convert to the metric system. However, the government was not prepared to accept our amendments. The minister has been asked questions from time to time, and on May 3 the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) put a question to the minister, as reported at page 5526 of Hansard, which I should once again like to place on record. He asked:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of State (Small Business). In view of the acceleration of widespread protest emanating from the producers of western Canada against the conversion to metric in the grains industry, is the minister giving any consideration whatsoever to the various representations he and other members have received and has he now reached the conclusion that the producer organizations upon which he relied when considering this particular piece of legislation did not actually reflect the wishes of the producers in western Canada?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, without accepting all the premises of the question, I want to say to the hon. member that I have been listening to the representations members made to me and the government, and particularly more recently to the representation made to me by the Minister without Portfolio from Crowfoot and-
Then there were some interruptions. The hon. minister continued:
-and other members of parliament on this side of the House from the prairie region. A decision has been made not to proclaim that section of the bill on metric conversion relating to the grains industry-
Then followed further interruptions, and he continued:
-until after further consultation-
A little later he went on to say that he would be pleased to have the views of members on this side as to the form that this consultation should take. We on this side of the House told the minister what form the consultations should take. In fact, we moved a motion a short time ago asking that certain sections of the bill be referred back to committee, with the idea that the committee could go out to western Canada and receive representations from the concerned people-the farmers and the grain producers. The hon. minister did not accept the amendment or the motion, neither has he accepted our recommendation.
[DOT] (U20)
I assume his intention is to send out representatives of the metric commission who have a vested interest in the bill and want to see it go through. It would not be an open-minded committee prepared to sit down with the farmers and listen to

their views. The committee would go out to western Canada and spend its time trying to do a selling job to the farmers and persuade them of the fine system contained in this bill. This is not the type of consultation we feel should take place. I should point out that this is our feeling as to what the minister might do.
He has asked for our recommendations. He has said that he wants to have consultation. Well, he has had plenty of opportunity to stand in this House and make a speech telling us what he plans to do. Despite the length of time this bill has been debated in the House, the minister has not been prepared to stand and tell the House and the western farmers about his plans. Because of the fact that he has been silent on the issue, we in the official opposition have proposed a referral back to committee of certain sections by way of the motion we are debating now, a six months' hoist.
I see my time is running out, but I would like to challenge the minister to stand in this House and tell us what he plans to do as far as the consultative process is concerned. He may have plans which we will find acceptable. If so, we will deal with the bill with dispatch. On the other hand, if he is not prepared to stand and tell us what his plans are, and if he says that he is sending a delegation of public servants out to the west, I can assure him this bill will not be dealt with quickly. The western members on this side feel so strongly about this bill that we are prepared to spend a good portion of the summer debating it in this House.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few additional remarks in this debate because it is a matter of great importance to western Canada and to the farmers in my constituency. What we have here is an example of a Liberal government demonstrating mule-headed stubbornness in the face of widespread opposition to the proposal which it is putting before the people and it is not desired by the people who will be affected. We have a situation where this mule-headed stubbornness of the Liberal party is wasting the time of this institution by debating an issue for so long, the result of which should be obvious to the government.
The Liberal government refuses to pay any attention to the feelings and the representations which have been made by concerned farmers. As I have said, this governmnet is wasting the time of the House of Commons with this bill, which is a very serious breach of its duties to the people of Canada. Everybody in this country will accept and admit that we are faced with many serious and difficult problems which need to be dealt with by the parliament of Canada, yet these problems are not being discussed in this place because we are tied up with a bill which should not have been presented in the first place. The unity of the country is in severe jeopardy. This jeopardy arose during the tenure of this government, and they totally refuses to come to grips with it.
During previous hearings on this bill at committee stage, and indeed in this House, we were told by the minister that the bill was supported by farm organizations-the National Farmers Union, the Federation of Agriculture, and so on. In committee I found that the representatives of these organizations
June 16, 1977

supported the bill, much to my surprise because I have not found any farmers who support it. 1 see the minister woke up from his nap when I said that the farm organizations are supporting the bill. After consultation with the representatives of the National Farmers Union and other farm organizations, we found that they did not consult with farmers. What happened is that the government bamboozled these organizations into thinking that the content of the bill was actively in effect in this country and that any opposition to it would be totally futile. The government also indicated that it was just a matter of simple housekeeping.
Under' these circumstances, the farm organization representatives decided there was no need to consult with the producers and the constituents because the bill was a fait accompli and nothing would be gained by it. That is an example of the government being dishonest with these organizations by telling them there was no use in objecting. The organizations felt that if that was the case they might as well let the thing go and get used to it. Thus, they did not object.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: You should tell the farm organizations that.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, I did tell the farm organizations that. They indicated that in response to questions I put to them in committee. I do not think the minister was present at that time, so I would suggest he read the testimony which was put forth. On the same day, the National Federation of Agriculture was meeting in Ottawa and they refused to take a position, in consultation with the delegates there, because they did not want to go against the testimony which had already been given by their representatives. At the same time, they did not want to approve the legislation the minister was putting forward. On that occasion it was decided to simply table the issue and try to make a decision on another day.
If one reviews the correspondence which has been received directly from the producers, it is obvious they are not in favour of the measures in this bill. The producers are not in favour of metrication because there is nothing to be gained. They are not putting forward the argument that in general there might not be benefits for the manufacturing sector which is involved in export, for example. The producers are not necesarily arguing that certain mathematical calculations are not simple when they are carried out in the metric system. The fact is that these things are not all that important in so far as any advantages to the farmer are concerned.
Obviously, the farmers are objecting to this measure on the basis that changing acres to hectares, or bushels to tonnes, is a totally useless and unnecessary change. It will not in any way increase their productivity. It will simply add to the emotional pressure of farming under bad economic conditions which farmers are already facing. Indeed, it will add to the confusion and disorder in their lives which has resulted largely from actions of this government in the past on other issues. If one looks at this objectively and unemotionally, he will easily see
Metric System
that a change in weights and measures in so far as the agricultural producer is concerned is of no value at all.
There are some supporters of metrication. We hear the argument everywhere that it will simplify the life of Canadians. 1 have stated before that it might do that in some limited areas. However, when we consider the measurement of land and grain, and the fact that people involved in the agricultural industry have their minds and their brains trained and adjusted to thinking in the system used until now, it is almost impossible to justify the additional burden which will result from this change. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) described it well when he said it was simply a bureaucratic attempt to force everyone to conform for no other reason than to have conformity in the world. In my view, conformity is not always the best way to go.
We have a situation where the government has taken the position that it is the master, rather than the servant, of the people. That points out very clearly the difference between Progressive Conservative philosophy and Liberal philosophy. The Liberals always take the position that they know what is best for the people, that they are smartest and that they must impose their views on the people for their own good. The Conservatives believe that a democratically elected representative is sent to Ottawa to speak in the House of Commons on behalf of those who elected him. The Conservative party and Conservative governments in the past have always taken the position that government is the servant of the people and that the master is people themselves. We must always remember that, if democracy is to survive.
The position taken by the Liberal administration, that it is the master, is a grave distortion of a very important democratic principle. It brings into question whether democracy exists at all. When you ignore the views of the majority of people and impose your views upon them, it shows that you are a government too weak-kneed to withstand the bureaucratic pressure to change to conformity in the world. I have already said that conformity is not necessarily the best way.

speechtext:
The minister made an interjection which I did not fully hear. I hope that when I resume my seat he will stand and explain why he takes the position that he is the master of the people and does not have to pay any attention to the representations being made to him. Perhaps he has a reason for that, although I doubt whether it would be a logical reason if he believes in democracy.
This is not the only bill wherein the government is intruding more and more into the daily lives of Canadians, creating greater and greater erosion of the democratic principle that government must serve the people. There are other examples where democracy has been severely eroded. One need only look at the rule changes in this House since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came into power. When the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister, there were happy times in Canada. The economy of this country

boomed. Everyone in the country felt they had some sort of a goal toward which they were heading, as opposed to the present, rudderless ship floating in any direction the wind will take it. That is the policy of this government.
Democratic principles have been eroded in so far as the authority of parliament is concerned. During the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, question period was an occasion when government truly accounted to the representatives of the people in this House for their actions, policies and how they spent Canadians' tax dollars. Question period at that time was an accounting session which went on as long as anyone had any useful questions to ask.
The opposition of that day, which is now the government, used the question period to destroy the government of the day and throw it out of power. When they got into power, they realized what a valuable democratic tool the uncontrolled question period was. They immediately decided to put a limit on the length of the question period, thereby reducing the risk to themselves in so far as concerned being exposed to any meaningful attack in the House.
On the departure of the former prime minister, Mr. Pearson, and the arrival of the present Prime Minister, it was taken a step further. Ministers were removed from the House for two or three days a week, and the ability to call on ministers and the government to account for their actions and policies was curtailed even further. The people of Canada revolted against that and nearly threw them out in 1972. That was the time the Prime Minister decided to bring his ministers back into the House. However, they now follow a policy of not answering or accounting in a meaningful way to the representatives of the people who ask questions of them in this House during question period.
There is another example with regard to accounting to the people as to how their tax dollars are spent. Prior to the rule changes in 1969, parliament had the right to hold up the expenditures of the government if it did not provide proper answers with regard to how the tax money was being spent. That is no longer a right of parliament; that right has perhaps been lost forever. Now, on a certain date the expenditure items, the estimate.s, go through automatically.
The result of this change has been an accelerated rise in the federal budget and an accompanying rise in the taxation imposed upon the people of Canada. In the short period of eight or nine years there has been an increase from $10.8 billion to some $45 billion. That is one of the largest single contributing factors to the severe inflation in this country. As I said before, it is an erosion of the democratic right of the people to call on this government to account for its actions with regard to how it spends the tax money that it takes from people who work very hard.
This legislation affects the culture of the people of Canada. The system which a society uses to determine its weights and measures is, indeed, one aspect of its culture. If we look at it from that point of view, we have a situation in which this

government, through its legislation, is attempting to change the culture of Canada. We know from experiences in Europe and in other places that governments are not to be trusted with trying to change the culture of a country and controlling the development of culture. Culture, to be meaningful, must arise from the people themselves and must evolve and develop in accordance with the natural evolution that takes place in a country, given certain freedoms and rights to which individuals are entitled.
It seems to me that the House, if it is to be representative of the people of this nation, must consider the interests of the farmers in this case above the interests of the grain handling industry. It is much simpler for the conversion to be made by the grain handling industry than for the farmer to make the conversion, because it is only the grain handlers who are involved in international trade and export-so why not let them make the conversion? Why impose the conversion on the producer who is not directly involved in international trade and the exportation of his product?
The other point which I think is very important is that in the measurement of land the minister insists we change from acres to hectares. We will not be exporting land, so we cannot use the export argument to insist on changing land measurements.

speechtext: Alberta and Saskatchewan have put forward legislation. The Ontario legislation is of a permissive type. The Alberta legislation was never proclaimed. It is only Saskatchewan, I understand, that has passed, by order in council, and proclaimed legislation which would conform to what the minister is proposing. Nevertheless, if it were not for this bill I doubt very much that the provinces would proceed on their own to make these changes. So if the minister is trying to blame the provinces for making these changes, he is being a little less than honest-and I expect more than that from him.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: It is a co-operative effort.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: I have known the minister for some time. He came to the House at the same time as I did, and I have never known him to be dishonest in the past. Now he is putting the responsibility on the provinces. I am sure he is aware of the heat this legislation is creating. It is uncomfortable for him, so he is attempting to say that the provinces are making these changes. I think that if he wants to take that position there is no point at all in talking to him, because he is missing the whole point of what we are trying to say and is excusing himself completely from playing any serious role in what is happening here.

speechtext:
Indeed, the minister himself, when the hon. member for Crowfoot crossed the floor, proclaimed very proudly that he was now consulting closely with the hon. member for Crowfoot in this matter and that his representations would be considered. If the minister is trying to tell us now that the hon. member for Crowfoot has changed his mind about metrication in so far as farmers are concerned, I would be very surprised if that were the case, because that hon. member spoke very vigorously against metrication when he was on this side of the House, and I believe he still feels the same way.
So the question arises as to whether the government will be using the hon. member for Crowfoot for its own purposes, or whether it will be using him for hearing representations from the people of Alberta. We know from past experiences with Bud Olson, for example, the former minister of agriculture who, while sitting in the cabinet of this government must have been a very frustrated man, what happened to him as a result of the fact that the government had used him. We know that he was aware of the views of the people of Alberta, of the views of farmers in Alberta and, perhaps, in western Canada. There is no doubt about that, because I talked to that hon. member on many occasions. But he was not able to convince the Liberal cabinet that the views of the western farmers in Alberta were worth considering. Instead, the Liberal cabinet chose to use the minister as their mouthpiece to impose their views, once again, on the people of the west, and indeed he had to try to explain away policies which were unexplainable and unacceptable to the people in that area. So the people decided to throw him out.
I predict that if this Liberal cabinet attempts to use the hon. member for Crowfoot as a tool for imposing their own views on the people of the west, rather than to use him as a resource person to hear representations from the west, the people will throw him out, too-and any other member who takes the position that he might be able to be effective within the Liberal ranks. So I think the minister should give that some thought. He should put it in his pipe and smoke it.

I am sure that if he did that he would come back to the House and tell us that this bill is no good, that it should be changed, that it should reflect the desires of the people it will affect. Mind you, I am saying that on the assumption that the minister believes in democratic representation. If the minister believes in democracy and that the representations of people should be considered by the government, he should say that. He has not said it so far.

It may indeed be visible in so far as manufacturers are concerned, but when you consider the cost of the metrication bill, the financial cost of imposing metrication on the country-which is in the vicinity of $5 billion-you begin to wonder why this government is anxious to spend so much money on this conversion which is undesirable and which will not change anything so far as the producer is concerned.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
We are imposing a $5 billion price tag on the people of Canada who are already taxed to death. Everybody in a democratic society will accept the fact that some taxes are necessary because we need an army, highways, airports and services of that kind. But in this country we have a situation where 43 per cent of the gross national product is already in the public domain. Various governments take that percentage of the gross national product for their own purposes. That is already a dangerously high amount. It is much higher than is

June 16, 1977

acceptable in a democratic system based upon private enterprise and individual initiative.
Imposing an additional $5 billion price tag will increase that 43 per cent to a substantially higher amount. We know we cannot go very much higher without stifling individual initiative. People are saying they have to give a lot to the government, anyway, and they are wondering why they should work any harder or increase their productivity or income. So we have inflation in this country. We have a situation in which productivity is already behind other countries. We have almost priced ourselves out of the international markets, and this will only be one step further in that direction. This measure will stifle initiative because increased taxation will be necessary to implement it.
The mental confusion which will result while people are trying to convert in their own minds is bound to result in decreased productivity. Productivity will decrease in two ways as a result of conversion. It will decrease because taxes will go up to pay the bill, and it will decrease because of the mental confusion there will be until conversion is made within the brains of the people of Canada.
I think the government is in a position now where it must rededicate itself to cutting down its own costs and to reducing taxes, rather than continuing to dedicate itself to finding ways of spending more and more money of Canadians, thereby raising taxes to a greater extent when we know that they are already too high. We must be looking for ways to increase productivity so that we can be competitive on international markets. We should not be trying further to reduce our competitiveness in international markets, because we know that if we are going to survive as an industrialized nation in a very competitive industrialized world, we must make ourselves more competitive.

If this government cared even a little about what the Canadian people really want, it would have gone to the people for a mandate by way of a national referendum. We asked for a referendum on whether the people of Canada want bilingualism, and we asked for a national referendum on the issue of capital punishment. We cannot get a referendum, Mr. Speaker; but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) invites the government of Quebec to hold a referendum on the question of a province separating from confederation and jeopardizing the future of our entire nation. There is no doubt that we will have to accept the government's whole package of metric, including the imposition of the metric scale on our agricultural community, because those members on the other side of the House close their eyes and vote however their leader orders them to vote. They would vote to instal Idi Amin as their deputy leader if the Prime Minister ordered them to do so. All we can hope for is to convince the government that there are segments of our economy that would suffer to such an extent that they would need government assistance and understanding in order to survive this latest onslaught on their capabilities.
I am thinking in particular of the small business community and of the financial burden being placed on them by the conversion to metric. Small businesses in Canada are caught in a web of circumstances, none of which are due to their actions or their lack of action. They are being subjected to harassment and hassling from various government agencies and bureaux, with growing demands for reports, fees and charges. The small business community depends on the Post Office to a greater extent than any other single segment of our society, and it is no secret that they are constantly being let down in that quarter. For some businesses, as 1 pointed out in this House last Monday, the Post Office is a lifeline. When that lifeline is cut, as it so often is these days, many of those businesses go under.

We are losing too many small businesses in Canada today because of irregular and unreliable postal service. Those businesses which can afford to have already turned from the Post Office to private courier services. The Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) and the postal unions complain about the business they are losing to the private courier services-but it is their own fault. I can foresee an even greater use of the private courier systems in the future because the Canadian postal service continues to get worse.
Last Monday, when we were debating the amendments to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, I pointed out that the imposition of the metric system would work a hardship on people involved in those types of activities. The government said at the outset of the metric debate that businesses and industries affected would have to absorb the costs involved in converting to the new system. Later we were told that some adjustments would be made so that small businesses, for example, would be assisted financially in making the conversion.
The fact remains, though, that the greater share of the cost of conversion will fall on the shoulders of small businessmen, fishermen and farmers. In Monday's debate I suggested that many small business people would be hard pressed to come up with the money to pay the cost of conversion, in view of all the other demands on their capital, the ravages of inflation, higher production and labour costs and a multitude of other demands on their resources. I urged the government to take this into consideration and to bring in a more flexible small businesses loans plan. I said that many of these small business people would have to borrow money to pay the cost of converting their equipment to the metric system. But on reflection I wonder whether they should have to borrow money at high rates of interest to pay the cost of something that they did not ask for, something about which they were not even consulted by the government or anyone else.
The small business community in Canada did not ask for the metric system; the fishermen did not ask for it; the farmers did not ask for it. In fact, the Canadian people did not ask for it, nor were they ever consulted about it. It has been imposed upon all of us, and the real reason why it was imposed upon us has never been told. I doubt that it will ever be told.
As far as the cost of converting small businesses is concerned, there are only two acceptable ways this can be dealt with. One is for the federal government to pick up the tab for the conversion costs. After all, it was the federal government's idea in the first place. If they want farmers, fishermen and small business people to play this expensive and ridiculous game, they should be prepared to pay their way into the ball-park.
The other way this might be accomplished at a minimum of direct cost and inconvenience to small businesses is to extend long-term, no-interest loans to defray conversion costs. If we can make long-term loans at little or no interest to countries like Cuba, and if we can make grants to countries on the far side of the earth to improve their farms and businesses, we can

Because our football players would have to attain a greater distance on the football field, which could be measured in metres or centimetres, the Canadian game might have to resort to four downs and under present rules, with markings ten yards apart, we are having a difficult enough time achieving three downs. That is why we use the pass so much. But if we went to four downs we would find it relatively easy, under the metric system, to achieve the first down, because under the four downs system a player can usually achieve 11 yards.
If we played the four downs game, which involves some extra distance, it would be said we had too much offence and not enough defence. Therefore, we would have to rule out our motion in the backfield, a unique feature of the Canadian game. In other words, if we make our football game conform to the metric system, we shall need to adopt American rules to offset the disadvantage. That is why we would not go for it. Our Canadian game is unique. Remember, the Americans imported their game from the colony of Canada. They played the first organized game when our team from McGill played an American university team south of the border. Our team played under our rugby rule which allowed for the carrying of the ball. But that rule was not part of the game of rugby which came to their shores from England. The Americans adjusted to the Canadian game. I point out that the Canadian game has a unique history.

The metric system is designed for those with purely technical needs. If we adopt it, we are not going to change some of our idiomatic expressions. A foot will still be a foot, and our numerous remarks which relate to the old measurements will still be part of our culture. I say, let us not be illogical in our opposition. If you have real complaints about the metric system, make them, because I do. 1 do not find the minister unreasonable. He listens to what I say. No provision has been made for the mechanics of the country; no provision has been made for the farmers; no provision has been made for small business. How can the government ever believe it will get the support of the public and retain respect for parliament? We have depreciated this institution to such an extent that soon no one will care one whit about it: it will have been depreciated to the point at which a great many Canadians will hope it will disappear. subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
That the Anti-Inflation Act being chapter 75, Statutes of Canada 1974-75-76, as amended by chapter 98, Statutes of Canada 1974-75-76 shall expire on the 30th day of June, 1977,
He said: Mr. Speaker, our motion today is prompted by the increasing evidence that the Canadian economy continues to deteriorate at an alarming pace. Real growth is below expectations, inflation and unemployment are above expectations and our competitive position in the world has fallen, as evidenced by a $10 billion end-products trade deficit in each of the last two years, almost triple the 1971 level.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
We have been lulled into believing that debt is a substitute for real wealth. With our foreign borrowings now at $50 billion, or approximately $5,000 for each of our workers, we have become the world's greatest debtor. Unfortunately, much of this current international borrowing has been to pay for consumer goods and services, creating the illusion we are wealthier than we really are. As a nation we are not on the right course.
This government's budgetary thrusts have misfired. Forecasts have not materialized. In his May 25 budget last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said, "The Canadian economy will generate more than 250,000 new jobs this year." He was referring to 1976. Yet from December, 1975 to December, 1976 only 67,000 jobs were created, a 73 per cent shortfall.
The minister stated further that "Unemployment will gradually decline as cyclical expansion takes hold." Instead, unemployment rose to a 37-year high, while United States unemployment is at a 30-month low.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext: And the government will not stay to listen.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
A factor contributing to this economic malaise is the government's reluctance to drop its wage and price controls which are not only working poorly but which are deterring the formation of investment capital and the creation of jobs. I would say this to whoever might be inclined to vote against our motion and, in effect, for a continuation of controls: He or she should go down to the local unemployment offices and look squarely in the eye the people who are being condemned to further unemployment.
It is no accident that we are now experiencing the highest unemployment rate of any industrialized nation. It is not just happenstance that in each of our five eastern provinces the level of unemployment is higher than that of any state south of the border. It is due to poor economic direction on the part of
Anti-Inflation Act
this administration and its officials, including those at the Bank of Canada. It is time to stop using Canada as a test tube or guinea pig for Galbraithian theories. It is time we put an end to wage and price controls in their present form.
Against this background and with mounting evidence that wage and price controls are not working, the onus is upon the administration, and in particular upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), today, tomorrow and Monday, to justify the continuation of controls. Oddly enough, we have already heard a great deal of evidence from the Prime Minister and his ministers that in today's economic environment controls should be terminated. And there is very little evidence from the same sources that they should be continued. I intend to present some of this evidence and refer to some of those statements later in my remarks. When we compare statements made by the Prime Minister on the subject of controls with those made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) we find that over the years the Prime Minister has tended to say whatever he feels would further his own political interests, irrespective of the facts. Sometimes he has been in favour of controls, sometimes against them. But through it all he has been consistently inconsistent. The Minister of Finance has showed more candour, consistently maintaining that we should be out of controls as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, the government's wage and price program has been nothing more than a cruel hoax on the Canadian public. Three years ago in the 1974 election, hon. members will recall that the Prime Minister was peddling a beautiful potion called "Trudeau Liberalism". On that occasion, this patent medicineman described controls as "a disaster looking for a place to happen". Today there can be no confusion as to what controls, as instituted by the government, have and have not done. They have failed effectively to contain inflation which after 20 months is now running at an annual rate of 10.4 per cent, only 2/10ths of one per cent lower than the 10.6 per cent annual rate when controls were first applied. Even the administration admits that this year's target for inflation will not be met and has given up completely on next year's target of 4 per cent. It is becoming just another embarrassing memory.
Controls have, however, been effective in deterring real economic growth and they have stifled the creation of jobs for hundreds of thousands who are out of work. I could read into the record opinions expressed by many of our nation's leading figures, all calling for an end to controls-people like former deputy finance minister Simon Reisman or labour's Ron Lang. "Think tanks" like the Fraser Institute and the C.B. Howe Institute all believe, as we do, that the process of decontrol should begin immediately. But the most appropriate source from which to quote today is the Prime Minister. I do not believe anybody could say it any better than he did when he told a Nova Scotia audience that controls "create far more problems than they solve" or when he said "the economies which have been subjected to this straitjacket of freeze and controls have not performed better on inflation and have themselves been turning in very poor performances".

June 16, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
It is precisely those two effects produced by controls- marginal success in fighting inflation and stifled economic performance-which are the basis of my party's challenge to the government to begin the decontrol process, not next month, not next year, but now. I believe we should take the Prime Minister at his word when he told a St. Catharines audience that "the real way to fight inflation is not to put a straitjacket on the economy; not to throttle the worker or farmer, or the producer or the storekeeper; not to bring in a system of hocus-pocus magical solutions." 1 hope the Prime Minister will remember his words when he said: "If a government cannot cope with self-induced inflation it deserves to be thrown out."
The plain truth is that whatever marginal success we have had in the battle against soaring costs has been due to the competitive process in the private sector. The Minister of Finance himself made this clear in committee recently. He said, and I quote: "Indeed, prices have been held down as much by the competitive factor as by the anti-inflation program." To make the situation doubly clear, he added: "May I correct that? It was more by competitive factors than by anti-inflation programs."
In the light of the minister's admission that it is the private sector, not the Anti-Inflation Board, which is containing prices, why are we still rigidly locked into wage and price controls? Why is the government not moving quickly to dismantle a system which has created very serious distortions in our economy, distortions which are evident from the flight of investment capital to the United States and our miserable record in job creation? We on this side suspect that the Trudeau administration is playing politics with our nation's economy-that it is abdicating its responsibility for leadership and is once again fashioning another of its great misrepresentations. The government knows that now is the time to get out of controls. The Minister of Finance said in February that the economic situation "would appear to give us the green light for decontrol" and he reaffirmed this view in committee two weeks ago. The government knows this. Yet it is stalling because the Prime Minister does not know how it should be played politically. Such lack of leadership is dangerous. The government realizes that controls should be lifted. The Minister of Finance said he hopes they are lifted sooner rather than later because of the concern he feels might exist regarding distortions which could arise. In short, the government seems to be torn between economic realities and sheer political expediency.
In suggesting today that the decontrol period should commence on June 30, let me make one thing clear. We are not as hard on controls as the Prime Minister was when he chose to be against controls in 1974. We believe that controls can be used for a limited period in connection with proper fiscal restraint, monetary restraint, and above all if there is a disposition on the part of government to deregulate the economy. Such imposition of controls, however, I would emphasize, should be temporary and they must be administered in an equitable fashion. To this end, the controls must have a

certainty so that they will be clear to all who wish to abide by them. They must never appear to favour one group or one sector or one person over another group, sector or person.
So far today, Mr. Speaker, I have attempted to establish that Canada's economic realities dictate that decontrol should begin on June 30. Over and above that, it is important to remember that this administration's wage and price controls program has not met the essential ingredients of an effective wage and price controls program. When the administration announced their current wage and price controls, they referred to fiscal restraint and monetary restraint. They said that there was a need to deregulate the economy. This has, in fact, not happened. There has been little restraint on the part of this government, and what restraint we have had has been unintentional.
In recent months the government has had no alternative but to be restrained, because frankly it has run out of revenue. The government's own planning is so far off course that it simply has nothing left to spend. The record budgetary deficit of $7.1 billion this year is a response not to today's problems but to yesterday's mistakes, and the restraint the government talks about is really the result of running out of revenue.
When the minister talks of breaking the inflationary psychology, I suspect he really means that he has at long last discovered the bottom of the taxpayer's pocket. No less than Gerald Bouey, governor of the Bank of Canada, has spelled out the significant role of government in causing inflation in this country. In the November 1975 Bank of Canada Review, Governor Bouey had this to say: "There is no great mystery about the nature and origins of our current economic difficulties." They are, he said, the result of the pursuit of "very expansionary monetary and fiscal policies". "The current wave of inflation", he added, "was not initiated by a marked acceleration of wage and salary increases". Nevertheless the Governor supported wage and price controls provided they were applied in tandem with a policy of monetary and fiscal restraint.
Have we had such restraint? We all know that government spending plans have jumped 28 per cent since the middle of 1975. Such government spending increases are, of course, not reflected in the consumer price index but in the nation's broader index, known as the deflator. There we find that between the third quarter of 1975 and the end of last year, government prices jumped 15.2 per cent in Canada, or about one per cent a month. Some fiscal restraint!
So far as monetary restraint is concerned, perhaps the simplest way to put it is that in September, 1975 just before controls began our banks had total Canadian assets, including Canadian deposits, of $73 billion. By March of this year those assets had exploded to $92 billion, or 25 per cent more than they were 18 months previously. That represents roughly an increase of 1.4 per cent per month. To suggest that that is monetary restraint, with real growth in this country running in the same period at something between 5 and 6 per cent, is ludicrous.
June 16, 1977

Now let me deal with government rhetoric about deregulating the economy. On October 14, 1975 the minister, when presenting the anti-inflation package, said:
We propose to scrutinize a wide variety of government policies and programs in an effort to find ways of reducing rigidities and costs that may impose unnecessarily on various sectors of the economy.
In the 20 months which have ensued there has been no meaningful review of government spending programs or of their effect on the regulation of business. Rather than deregulate the government is in fact proposing still greater regulation of industry. In this connection I refer hon. members to two bills both coming out of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Bill C-16, which is now before a committee of this House, proposes to regulate the finance industry in certain ways. Obviously, it has been drafted by a person who does not understand the financial world, so much so that to date the minister has offered 75 amendments to the bill in committee. Yet notwithstanding that bungling, the minister admits that should the bill be passed it will require 25 additional civil servants, at a cost of $500,000, to administer this program of regulation.
The same minister has Bill C-42 before another committee, the so-called competition bill. There we find it is proposed to appoint an "economic czar" to rule on various business matters in this country. We find this project will require the hiring of 80 civil servants further to regulate the industry, at a total cost of $2 million.
I cite those two examples of further proposed regulation because it is of interest to note that when the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was established by the former minister of the department, John Turner, in 1968, he pointed out that the net cost of the department was $2 million and that he did not anticipate this expenditure would rise. Today, we find it has blossomed into a department employing 3,027 civil servants and has a net budget of $61 million. In those few years, Mr. Speaker, the budget has grown from a net of $2 million to $61 million. Where is the deregulation which the government has said is part of its anti-inflation program?
I have cited the example of one department, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; I could cite many others. I could go through department by department and show the constant intrusion into the business affairs of Canadians which this governent insists upon. This can be seen in the growth of the Anti-Inflation Board itself. It has grown four and a half times from its original size and now costs the taxpayers of Canada $12 million in salaries alone.
Ending the Anti-Inflation Board would be one step, in our opinion, in restoring competition in our economy, in restoring meaningful collective bargaining, in restoring the proper balance between the public and the private sectors. Incidentally, the private sector is the source of wealth and the wellhead of jobs for most people in Canada. The ending of the AIB would also be one step in the deregulation of our economy and the restoring of confidence in the business community of Canada today.
Anti-Inflation Act
Having said that, I emphasize that our position with respect to the motion today has been consistent. In October, 1975 when the government first proposed the anti-inflation legislation which we are now considering we made it clear that we felt its timing was wrong but that we would go along with the government if it would assure us that the program would be for a relatively short period of time, and in any event for not longer than 18 months. They refused to give us that assurance which caused us to vote against the legislation at every stage. We were frightened they were proposing to bring in controls for a relatively lengthy period of time in Canada. We originally supported 18 months, and now it is 20 months. All the evidence suggests that the country would be better off without the controls in their present form. The experiment is over, if you like, and it is time for the government to retreat from their intervention in the marketplace. The experiment has failed.
As I have said, if you have controls, then the essence of the program must be one which the people feel is equitable. They must feel it applies to the rich, the poor, businessmen, the worker, the farmer and the processor. This program has never had that general confidence which is needed to make a wage and price control program work properly. This program is not a control program. If you analyse it, it is rather like a loose-fitting lid which tends to perpetuate inflation, as much as it tends to control inflation.
In the United States, which has no controls, inflation is currently running at 6.8 per cent. We in Canada face inflation of 7.8 per cent. How could it be otherwise? Once the government suggests that everybody is entitled to an 8 per cent or a 6 per cent increase, plus 2 per cent for productivity and 2 per cent for catch-up-a total increase of 10 per cent or 12 per cent-you have given the negotiators an excuse to say they will accept the 10 per cent or 12 per cent, and then the haggling begins as to how much over those two levels the negotiators can extract from the others. Rather than settling a ceiling, the guidelines have become the floor for such settlements. In this context it may be more appropriate to say that the initials AIB stand for assured inflation base.
Not only is the controls program indefinite in its application, but there are glaring exceptions to the rules. The minister's own economic review, on page 30, vividly outlines the distortions which can be institutionalized in a program of this type. For example, we find that dentists received fees and incomes more than 19 per cent higher than their base periods. Despite the AIB guidelines limiting the increases to $2,400 a year, these and other professionals earned as much as $6,940 more in the reporting period than they did in the year before, almost three times the stated guidelines which others are asked to abide by. On the whole, professional incomes in all categories increased by 12 per cent or $4,890 which was twice the permitted level. The government says that this excessive income is due to the overlap in reporting periods, fiscal year ends and they may have worked harder. It may be, but the minister should tell that to the labourer who has been denied a 50 cent hourly raise on a $4 wage base. Tell that to the man

I believe those are some of the inequities which call for this program to be ended soon, namely June 30.
Another point I should like to touch on is the approach of government to their own spending increases. I have referred to salary increases, but it is also important to note what has happened to postal rates which went up 50 per cent. People have written to me, and I presume to other members of this House, concerning the 50 per cent postal rate and how it is justified. They have been told by the government that it is because we are losing too much money and our expenditures have gone up. What businessman could not say his expenditures have gone up if he was guaranteed a price hike of 50 per cent, if he felt that is all it would take to get that new price increase? The reasons for these astronomical increases may be justified, but I ask the government to consider the unmeasured cost of such disillusionment in our entire system. Think of the bitterness which will continue to grow when people sense the distortions being created by this AIB program. Whatever reasons or elaborate justifications the government can give for their own spending hikes or executive salary hikes, the man denied the 50 cent hourly increase will remember that the salaries of 29 top officers of Bell Canada will average $102,000 in 1977, an increase of $13,000 each over 1976.
There are distortions in the government's own spending programs. An example of that is user-pay. I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is present in the House. This is a favourite concept which he likes to espouse with respect to covering the deficits which have been run up mainly at Mirabel and in the Toronto airport situation.
I should like to cite one perhaps vivid example of the government practising anything but restraint, in spite of talking about restraint. I refer to the Bank of Canada's own Hall of Mirrors. How can we have faith in the federal government's so-called restraint when the Bank of Canada continues to build

Mr. Speaker, I thank the members of the House for their co-operation. I will attempt to be reasonably brief. I was referring to what I feel is a rather lavish demonstration of lack of restraint in the continuing construction of the Bank of Canada building on Wellington Street. The last estimate of the cost of that building which we had about a year ago was $55 million. We are currently trying to get new estimates. Apparently spending increases have been so unexpected that we cannot get a current accurate estimate of the total cost of that building.
I am simply saying that in the name of restraint, if nothing else is a symbol of restraint, I would have expected the government to have pulled back on the building of such a lavish financial building as is being built on Wellington Street. In fact, even at $55 million it means that the balance sheet value of the total real estate holdings of the Bank of Canada all across Canada is almost doubled by the cost of that one building.

Before coming to our proposals as to what should happen on June 30, 1 wish to briefly comment on what we fear may happen if the government continues with their present plan. We have been told by the Minister of Finance that he will announce before August a decontrol date. If you read the green paper, it is fairly clear that the program the government favours as far as decontrols are concerned is the so-called first-in first-out approach. In effect, that means corporations will be decontrolled in accordance with their fiscal year ends and labour contracts will be decontrolled at the date of their expiration.
I believe that if the government were pressed today, we would find that it was their current intention to announce a decontrol date as of January 1. When you think of it, that is a rather clever approach. Seventy per cent of the corporations have their year-end on December 31. This means that 70 per cent of the corporations in Canada will remain controlled until December 31, 1978. Fifty per cent of the labour contracts mature in the final quarter of the year. That means that 50 per cent of those contracts would be caught until virtually the end of 1978. That is one reason why we are pressing this motion today. We believe it is too long a period of time to be tying up the corporate side and the labour side of this country with the disjointed controls program that we now have.

We realize that there is apprehension among some, that when the present control program is ended and when decontrols become effective, there could be a flare-up with respect to either prices or wage settlements. We do not believe that will happen. However, we believe some mechanism should be put in place to ensure that there will be a minimum risk of that type of bubble flare-up or call it what you wish. To that end, we suggest with the dismantling of the present controls program on June 30 it should be understood that the rulings of the AIB or the administrator will continue to have effect for the term to which they apply. That is the first thing.
Second, we believe that price and wage developments from then on could be monitored by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. 1 have already indicated that they have a staff of some 3,000. Surely they would not have to add to their staff. That monitoring should ensure that if there are excessive price increases or wage settlements, public attention will be drawn to them.
We would suggest also that for the first six to 12 month period following decontrol day the largest corporations, the top 200 which represent approximately 54 per cent of the total production in this country, should be monitored by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In addition, there should be a 30 day advance notice given with respect to any price increase by those companies.
Likewise for the six to 12 months following decontrol day, June 30, we feel that unions representing workers in those largest corporations should be subject to a 30 day delay after settlement before the contract becomes effective. We feel this would allow for a public review of whatever the price or wage
Anti-Inflation Act
settlement might be. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) would then be able to draw public attention to anything he thought was excessive. If necessary, we suggest he should make a reference to the cabinet and, if necessary, the cabinet should accept the responsibility of rolling back either the price or wage settlement if they thought it was unduly excessive.
We emphasize that we believe this mechanism will at least ensure that there will not be the explosion in prices or wages that some fear, but which we do not fear, will occur after decontrols begin. However, should there be some kind of explosion, I believe it is right for the government to reserve the ultimate weapon of wage and price controls.
If for some reason the marketplace that has worked well in this country, certainly for decades, does not in the future work as well, government can reserve the right to impose wage and price controls at least for a temporary period. However, we believe that period is long gone as far as existing controls are concerned and they should be ended. We are stating the caution, if you like, that such a wage and price control program could be reimposed. That is the ultimate weapon the government should hold in order to ensure that there will not be unfair price or wage increases during the decontrol period.
That is our position. We urge hon. members to support the motion now before the House. We believe that with such a decontrol program, with meaningful fiscal restraint, monetary restraint and more deregulation rather than further regulation of Canadian industry that we can restore this country to a real growth of five or six per cent per year with a minimum of inflation and a minimum of unemployment. Canadians deserve it.
This can be one of the wealthiest nations in the world on a per capita basis. We as a nation, a government and a parliament must accept the challenge of delivering the real wealth that Canadians should have, not detracting from it as has happened to date.

Having said that as a polite preamble, I think it is important to underline that the majority of Canadians, both among organized and unorganized workers, despite the present inequity and distortions of the anti-inflation program, are prepared to support some form of incomes policy. I do not think there is any doubt about that at all. But they want a fair program, not one which largely ignores prices and profits while permitting executives to get a $60,000 a year increase.
Surely it must now be evident, even to the present government, that in the Canadian case-and that is the one we are talking about-salaries and wages were not the cause of the rampant inflation which led to the imposition of these controls in the fall of 1975. The evidence before 1975 clearly demonstrates this, and since that time inflation continues, while wages are the only element or our economy that is effectively controlled.
The A1B states that inflation will average over 7 per cent this year. Indeed, for the last four months inflation has increased at a rate exceeding 10 per cent. Who knows if it is going to stay at the 7 per cent level. There is very good reason to believe that the 10 per cent experience of the past few months can remain the common experience throughout the rest of this year. Food, oil and mortgage prices either remain high or continue to rocket upward. The real purchasing power of Canadian farmers is lower today than it was five years ago. These are the affects of the controls. Through the entire control period, when food is excluded from the consumer price index, the rate of inflation for every other element than food has continued to rise between 9 per cent and 11 per cent. In short, the program has simply not worked in terms of curtailing price increases. Canadian workers, I add immediately, have paid the price not once but twice over with this set of controls. Their incomes have been held down while the prices they pay increase. Any way you work the equation, ordinary Canadians, whether they are in the east or in the west or in southern Ontario, have been unfairly treated by this program.
Without spending much time today enumerating the many obvious inequities that are so evident in the program currently in place, I simply remind the House of the example I raised with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in the question period yesterday. I refer, of course, to the executive salary increases which, as I just indicated, are permitted to rise at the rate of $60,000 a year while ordinary Canadians, more than two million of whom live at the poverty level, are restricted to increases that cannot exceed $2,400. Such is the rough justice bestowed on the people of Canada by the Minister of Finance. Indeed, Canadians would have been unaware of the increases had I not drawn them to the attention of the Minister of Finance yesterday-our House leader referred a similar batch to the government's attention not long ago. Also, the Canadian people would not be aware of these horrendous increases had it not been for the American Securities and Exchange Commission which files reports on their firms' operations here in our country. Incredible? While incredible for normal people, it is not at all incredible in terms of the way the Liberal Party has governed this country.
The other example of unfairness, besides the obvious one in terms of salaries and wages, is the added penalty that Canadian women in particular have had to pay with this program, despite the platitudinous statements and provisions in the AIB regulations which permit increases designated to eliminate discriminatory pay practices. The board, in its first test on this question, shamelessly rolled back just such an award for Canadian women in the case of the Winnipeg Health Sciences Centre-surely a disgusting example of unfairness. The board

not only ignores workers and women's rights, but has also ignored its own published regulations.
As 1 said, I see no great need this afternoon to detail the program of obvious inequities. Rather we in the NDP feel it a responsibility upon us, in opposing this set of controls, this unfair AIB program, to provide some counter suggestions as to what should be put in its place. Despite the collective desire of the majority of Canadians to support government action in implementing an effective and fair form of incomes policy, this government in its green paper has clearly chosen to return to the status quo, to return to the same so-called free market system which has repeatedly led to either rampant inflation or unacceptable unemployment or, as the present situation sadly illustrates, to both high unemployment and high inflation.
When this government says, and 1 quote, "The market system is an efficient mechanism for allocating resources and it has great advantages in terms of the freedom of choice and scope for initiative that it offers," it is either being dishonest or, probably, hopelessly foolish. To claim that a forum for consultative action is going to change Canada s economic system one iota-as does the green paper-has the same truth value as the claim that inflation has been wrestled to the ground, or that separatism as a political movement in Quebec is dead. These are two equally "profound" observations which have been made by this government in the past.
It is important to note at this point in my argument that our economic system, in its essentials-I want to stress that-has remained unaltered by the controls. This controls program simply made a bad economic situation worse. It is clear both from the reiterated faith in the free market of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the green paper that the government plans simply to return to that status quo, as I said. But what is that status quo which in its essentials before the controls program, and after, has remained the same? Under controls, investment and pricing decisions are still made by the same people and largely in the same manner.
Under controls, unemployment continues to worsen and our national income remains grossly maldistributed. The situation has become marginally worse. Under controls, regional disparities still tear at the fabric of the nation and many of our natural resources continue to be misallocated, if they are not exported out of the country entirely. In short, Canadians find themselves in basically the same unfair economic circumstances today with these controls as they did without them. The prime difference is that with the controls the rhetoric justifying inequality has become even more hypocritical and offensive. My guess is that Canadians, at long last, have acquired a very healthy skepticism concerning the Prime Minister's shifting concepts of society. In 1968, we all remember with chagrin the "just society". Then we were launched on the search for the Prime Minister's new society. Before we could locate that, we were reintroduced to Mackenzie King's middle society in the throne speech. With the green paper, we will

now return to the status quo. Such is the dialectical process of Canadian liberalism.

Perceiving business unrest, and talk of a new society by the Prime Minister, the government sounded a thorough-going retreat from government planning by asserting its intention to allow free market forces to once again guide our economic destiny. Whether the Liberals can reassure the business community by retreating from suggestions of economic decision-making by the government remains to be seen. What is clear, however, is that the majority of Canadians want positive economic reform and positive economic leadership on the part of their governments. They want solutions, particularly to rampant inflation and to disturbing and sad unemployment. Our history clearly demonstrates that the so-called free market forces-contrary to what the Prime Minister has said, and contrary to what has been argued in the House this afternoon-have not, and cannot, solve Canada's economic difficulties. This wisdom has been learned even by middle-of-the-road parties all over the western world, except by such parties here in Canada.
Such forces, the so-called free market forces, will continue to fail in the future as they have failed in the past, and the Conservative promise of returning trust and confidence to a government where leadership will replace controls should be seen for what it is, a political assertion that a Conservative government would have precisely the same faith in free market forces as do the Liberals. The Conservative rhetoric differs; the substance, however, remains the same. The speech we heard from the Conservative party this afternoon confirms that in every detail.
Having made those observations, I want now to outline the New Democratic Party alternatives to our economic condition. In doing so, I want to make a couple of preliminary, straightforward and honest comments about the nature of inflation in Canada. First, because of the deep intermingling of our economy with that of the United States, much of our inflation in this country-I am tempted to say, most of it-is beyond our control. We trade in it by necessity, import it by proximity, and pay for it as the price of maintaining throughout our years a branch plant 17'conomy. Pretending to control inflation of this sort is to deny our existence, to deny our geography and to deny our past entrepreneurial inadequacies. It is simply to be dishonest to claim we can control that kind of inflation which we import.
The second point I want to make is that if we are to contend seriously and honestly with the effects of inflation, our government can, and should, provide some cushioning by ensuring that those unable to cope with inflation can at least be

June 16, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act compensated. In this connection I think particularly of those unfortunate Canadians living on welfare, and our pensioners. Most important of all are the steps the government can take to ensure that the Canadian economy is strong, resilient and able to continue functioning at full capacity without reflecting every twitch of the Dow Jones index on the New York stock exchange.
It is the position of the New Democratic Party that we should be looking to the establishment of a national incomes policy in the very near future. I want to stress in this context that a consciously pursued national incomes policy is inextricably linked with economic planning, as virtually every government in western Europe has discovered and, indeed, as the government of Japan has discovered. We cannot isolate ourselves from the rest of the world; but we can insulate our economy and make it more equitable with permanent economic planning at the national level. The national debate we should be having here this afternoon is one that should focus upon requesting the government of the day to take the lead in establishing the means by which Canadians can consciously seek to establish national planning and implement an effective incomes policy.
The fact is that we already have planning, we already have a controls system in the country, and they both work in a most haphazard and inequitable fashion shaped by a corporate dominated market economy. That is not simply left-wing political rhetoric; it is an economic description of the facts.

The Polish joke which was just made does not even merit comment. As I said, Mr. Speaker, no elaborate bureaucracy is required to implement the program. The mechanisms by which such a policy could be determined already exist in many government institutions. Every tax change or tax concession, each new tariff, a major subsidy or new transfer payment, every government decision affecting a commodity like oil, is part of an incomes policy. Change any of these elements and you change the size of the income, the rate of growth and the way it is shared among the people of Canada.
As I have said, the question before us, then, is not whether we should have planning and an incomes policy, but what kind

of planning and incomes policy we should have, and who should do the planning. The NDP, from its inception, has believed in the necessity of national planning in the economy. To assume that market forces would inherently achieve the common good is to believe that in a stampede mice need have no fear of elephants. It is as simple as that.
For the New Democratic Party there are three main ingredients in determining such a long-term policy in Canada. The first is the subject of investment allocation. Investment allocation obviously affects inflation and unemployment, as well as the rate and kinds of incomes growth in regions and for individuals. It is essential, therefore, that the national government play a leading role in investment policy. I reject the approach taken by the Conservative spokesman who categorically rejected government involvement in this regard.
I want to stress and to make clear that we do not want a cumbersome, inefficient, stultifying, centralized bureaucracy making all of our economic decisions. That is not how it works. While recognizing the authority and propriety of the national government to take decisive action in the economy for the public good, what is required is simply a planning authority in the Department of Finance. Such an authority, under government control, would interact with the private sector to ensure entrepreneurial efficiency and decentralized decision-making. Simply stated, what we require in Canada is a new national instrument to effect investment timing and priorities of the kind which have worked with great success for a number of years in Sweden. It would work in the following manner-
