Mr. Speaker, Conservatives have difficulty learning not only from books, but from other countries. Under such a proposal, each major firm would be required to deposit a portion of its profits in special firm-specific accounts with the government. Firms could spend the moneys in these accounts only at the times and for the purposes approved by the government. Thus, the government would not assume direct control over these funds. What is important is that it would have a significant means to directly influence the timing and direction of private sector investments. This is essential if we are to deal seriously with the inflation and unemployment which flow automatically from a market economy. I am talking about direct intervention in a mixed economy to reach the goals that the majority of the people desire-minimum levels of inflation and maximum levels of employment. That is how it can work.
Funds would be accumulated in periods of full employment and excess demand. They would be released in recessionary periods, to state the obvious. Thus, the cyclical nature and impact of the market economy could be significantly changed. Investment in regions of high unemployment would be given preference. Investment in housing would be encouraged. Investment in inventories could also be allowed in periods of slack demand. The business sector would accept that. In short, inflation and unemployment could be dealt with from within the framework of a set of national priorities established by the
June 16, 1977

national government. I repeat, in countries like Sweden we have seen this investment system work, and work well, both for the majority of the people and for the industry in the country. To a considerable degree, the private sector in Sweden supports and maintains precisely this kind of economic planning because they know it leads to an efficient, productive economy.
It is time we tried it here.
The other two elements for the NDP in determining a Canadian planning and incomes policy are to be found in employment and taxation programs. Today, both are high among the pressing issues of Canadian politics. We have a tragic unemployment problem and, with our existing tax laws, a hidden welfare system for the rich. I want to show how both are relevant to an incomes policy and to dealing in a serious way with a post-control society. By dealing with the unemployment problem, and by replacing the welfare system for the rich with a policy of taxation reform, we would be taking the necessary first steps toward a national incomes policy. The human consequence of unemployment is clear to all who want to look at the problem. I have no intention of repeating in today's debate the points 1 have made on other occasions about the human degradation that is involved when we have a system that allows 1 'h million Canadians to remain unemployed.
Apart from the human condition, the government has deflected our attention from the serious economic consequences of the unemployment problem in part by creating the economic myth that high rates of unemployment are inevitable and, therefore, the loss must be written off. The West Germans have not written them off, and the Japanese have not written them off. Only according to the Canadian government is high unemployment inevitable. We have been ignoring the fact that more than one million Canadians are not producing goods and services, nor are they receiving adequate incomes, and we have been ignoring the economic implications of this. Canada's unemployed are poorer for lack of work, poorer for lack of dignity that comes from work; so are we economically poorer as a nation because of this high level of unemployment.
The Liberals took from social democracy the idea and philosophy that our unemployed needed care; and I give the government credit for establishing a good unemployment insurance scheme. But, Mr. Speaker, they have ignored the even more basic social democratic requirement, namely, that we need an economic program of full employment. Social democrats in this country and elsewhere have always maintained that a fully employed, fully productive economy is a prerequisite of social and economic justice as a whole. You cannot have one without the other, in our view.
After 19 months of unemployment at rates over 7 per cent, the government can no longer hide the terrible drain on the economy-$6 billion annually in lost production of goods and services, $2 billion annually in unemployment insurance and welfare costs, and at least $1 billion in lost tax revenue. This level of unemployment and this lost production of goods and services has a direct and negative effect on levels of inflation. That is the point I want to make this afternoon. 1 have already put before parliament in this session detailed proposals for
Anti-Inflation Act
setting targets and timetables to achieve full employment over a three-year or four-year period. It cannot be done in a month.
It cannot be done in a year or two. To achieve full employment would take three or four years. We have made serious suggestions on how to achieve this objective.
The point I am making now is that there is a connection between increased production of goods and services, and inflation. The higher the production, the greater the likelihood of prices going down. More jobs, in short, with planning and other measures lead to less inflation. The other important element in sensible national planning that I want to talk about this afternoon is tax policy. Central to any incomes policy is a country's tax law. Our income tax system is in greater need of overhaul today than it was ten years ago when the Carter commission called for major reforms. The tax reform called for at that time has not only been ignored but has been reversed in application.
Corporate tax concessions unrelated to any specific economic benefit have continued in recent years in spite of criticism not only from those who believe in fairness but from those who believe in economic efficiency. I remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) this his predecessor commissioned his department to do a study. It concluded that special corporate tax concessions this government had introduced had not led to any positive net economic benefit for Canada. Social democratic governments of western Europe believe in a private sector, as does the New Democratic Party. But those governments do not give away billions of dollars to corporations as do the Canadian Liberals. A corporate tax concession in Sweden or West Germany depends on specific economic benefits. We need that system in Canada today.
The even more disturbing tax development of recent years is the extension of unjustified loopholes to personal income. This development has directly affected our ability to obtain support for an incomes policy. Every loophole, dodge or deferral accountants can think of has been written into the personal tax system, with the result that more than $6.4 billion is lost to the federal treasury every year, according to the National Welfare Council whose report published not long ago spells out in horrible detail how this system works. The report noted some 17 varieties of tax exemption open to and used by the rich in Canada.

improvements in collective bargaining in Canada. There is not a trade union in this country which would not welcome a reduction of the pressure-cooker atmosphere in which every round of bargaining is conducted at present. Union members would demand less wages if we had a fair and progressive tax system and the prospect of real growth in their income. The evidence in other countries shows that the idea works there. I am sure it would work here.
Canada can look forward to a stronger, more just economy in future only if we are prepared to acknowledge the need for the government to set national priorities which the majority of Canadians consider fair. If Canadian workers see fair taxes, lower mortgage rates and controlled energy prices, as they have them in other countries, they will co-operate with the government on an incomes policy. Unless the government embarks on the kind of planning I have suggested, in principle if not in detail, after our present controls come off we shall see a return in this country of the free market system which created precisely the difficulties from which we are trying to extricate ourselves.
Unless the government plans as I suggest, we shall revert to the boom and bust cycle which has plagued not only our market economy but that of every other developed country of the world. It will happen if the Liberals want to go back to those conditions. Let them not think they can deal with unemployment for a couple of years, drop that issue, deal with inflation for another couple of years, and so on, ad infinitum, ad nauseam; for I tell the Minister of Finance the people of Canada are tired of it. I say, on behalf of my party, a mixed economy can be made to work. We can deal with both unemployment and inflation simultaneously, as other countries have. But we cannot do it by burying our heads in the outdated thinking of the past, by allowing an unregulated economy to create problems for us in the future as it has in the past. We need sensible, tough-minded government planning. That is precisely what we say should take the place of the present controls.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the added opportunity to rise this afternoon, on behalf of my constituents in Richmond, to comment on the motion before us and the current government's anti-inflation program. Since the government launched that program, the economic situation of Canadians has remained on the same general course, that is on a steady decline. We will be told today, tomorrow and Monday that such unencouraging results are due to global economic conditions, that things are not so bad as the opposition would have it, that a five, ten or fifteen per cent increase in food costs is not too much because things would be worse had we not the Anti-Inflation Act.
The government side certainly will use the same statistics we have on this subject, but both sides will be making totally opposite points. We suggest that those figures, including those referred to by the sponsor of the motion, clearly point to the dangerous path Canada has been following. The government in turn will use the same figures to indicate how lucky we are to

get away at such little cost. Inflation certainly is bad in itself, but we must be weary of the opposite pitfall, letting things worsen by importing or letting big or multinational corporations import cheaper products from abroad, which would be importing unemployment. This would not abate inflation because the importing monopoly that buys cheaper abroad increases its profits rather than passing the saving on to the Canadian consumer.
So the one making the profit is the importer who can do as he pleases. I think the controls that were set up under the Anti-Inflation Act did not entirely manage to control importations. Here, I am placing myself in the boots of a guy in Richmond, for example, who will be asking himself when he reads about us-because we will be read tomorrow or this afternoon-if we really thought about him. I am wondering what the guy who was just laid off at Duchesse Shoe in Richmond, for example, is thinking, what the guy who was just laid off or is about to be laid off at Brown Shoe Co. (Canada) Ltd. in Richmond is thinking? I am wondering also what the copper mine worker in Stratford thinks of the effect of that anti-inflation law when there was an attempt to control the price of the metal. It was so much controlled that over 360 miners were laid off in the past year and a half. What was done to help them? Absolutely nothing, apart from giving a little bit of money to those who went to Canada Manpower Centres so they could move where there is another mine. Those 40 years of age and over were allowed to have a little unemployment under certain conditions, namely, that they report to two or three employers a week and be always asked the same question-are you looking for work?
Mr. Speaker, I think that all those questions are negative and do not lead anywhere. If the Anti-Inflation Act as set up by this government did not give better results, then it must absolutely be abolished. That Anti-Inflation Act must be repealed as soon as possible. In any case, we did not apply it to those who lend money, such as banks, to those who are already too rich. Banks are now richer than they ever were. They are making more money than they ever did. Money lenders before 1969 were getting 5 Vi per cent interest on first mortgages. That is the ordinary money lender. Last year, the same lender was getting \2lh per cent on first mortages for 75 per cent assessment, meaning he was lending 75 per cent of the actual value at 12'/2 per cent. That Anti-Inflation Act did not affect him at all. It affected the worker, of course, but it did not affect trusts at all.
Here I want to be direct, but not too harsh, because there is no point in it. I think suggestions must be constructive. I find that perhaps the Anti-Inflation Act affected dividends, perhaps certain areas of the stock market but did not go far enough as far as those who profit from little people, particularly little people who are exploited in an extraordinary way by any inflation, as the hon. member who spoke before me, the leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), suggested earlier. I think the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) also said the same thing. I think there is an attempt to extend the market to form some sort of common import-export market without
June 16, 1977

being too sharp on those controls. So they say that if we let footwear from Taiwan or elsewhere into Canada it is because that imported footwear costs 32, 33, 35 per cent less than the same footwear manufactured in this country. We are going to get it cheaper. That is wrong, wrong! As consumers we just have to go in any store-which 1 refrain from naming not to give them free advertising-in big anonymous chain stores which are the prime importers of footwear import in Canada and we will realize that shoes are becoming ever more expensive. Let us see what we were paying three years ago. For a pair of shoes manufactured outside this country and which comes from Taiwan, Japan, Czechoslovakia or elsewhere, and I have bills to prove it, we had to pay $33 and a few cents. Today that same pair of shoes imported from the very same places costs $54 in big chain stores. The government lets footwear enter the country in a flood as if there were no controls at all. It controls inflation because it is risky but it does not control the profits of the guy of the anonymous trust which makes a place for himself and against everybody. We dare not touch him.

speechtext: That one is not in the boat!

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
He is not in the boat of course! He is being controlled in a strange manner; perhaps he can be controlled by taxing profits. If it is a multinational corporation, it is very well controlled because one area of its activities is controlled, mostly if it goes through two or three countries before getting there; I will prove it to you in a few moments.
I should like to point out that subject to the House because that legislation affected everybody. Above all, there is one area which was not affected. The government made a large contribution to help the textile industry through that Anti-dumping Act and others-and it gets my admiration for that-because that was not an act but a regulation; that was a dumping measure.
The government took positive action, and again today one minister stood up to talk about that matter. I think that in textiles, in Quebec at least, things are improving and I commend the government for it. But in the shoe industry things have been going very badly for the last six or seven years. More specifically, June 4, 1970, as reported on page 7711 of Hansard, I was asking for the adjournment of the House precisely because the shoe industry was in dire straits. Mr. Speaker refused that motion because, though the matter was very important, it was not that urgent, and I quote:
The problem brought up by the hon. member for Richmond is certainly of national importance and worries several of his colleagues as well who have already shown, by means of repeated representations during the last weeks and months, that they are equally interested in this matter.
However, it seems to me that this very important problem drawn to our attention by the hon. member for Richmond does not have the urgency and immediacy required under Standing Order 26.
With the hon. member for Richmond and his colleagues, we must admit it is a problem national in scope, but it is important that a matter brought up under the provisions of Standing Order 26...
Anti-Inflation Act
.. .and so on, be of a new, urgent and sudden nature. The Chair was perfectly right, it was not a matter of sudden urgency, the footwear manufacturing industry had been in a poor situation for such a long time.
Under the circumstances, while acknowledging again the immediate and national importance of the problem raised by the hon. member, I respectfully suggest to him that it is not possible today to propose a motion asking for the adjournment of the House to discuss the problem which he pointed out.
Therefore, I followed the advice of the Chair and brought this matter up again and again during the next days and months.
On June 16, 1970, I asked under Standing Order 43 that a debate be held on the matter, but it was not allowed by a few members of the House. If I may I would like to quote an excerpt of my intervention as reported on page 8154 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the study of the question justifies an emergency debate considering that since January 1, 1970 shoe factories have been closing down at the fantastic rate of nearly one a week and, considering that between 1956 and 1969, Canada's footwear production has decreased by 1 per cent whereas imports have jumped by 568 per cent, considering that the industry now employs 3,260 fewer workers than in 1966 and considering also that the government seems to have lost control of footwear imports into Canada.
And I added:
On June 2, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) announced to the House that talks were under way about restrictions of footwear imports and I believe the same measure is urgently needed regarding the footwear industry.
As can be found at page 9009 of Hansard for November 13, 1975, I continued in that sense. Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up the time of the House with this, but I find that we have to repeat the same things over and over again in here, without any benefit for the producers or the workers in the shoe industry; that is unbelievable. That is why 1 want to say to hon. members that I know they are in good faith. But, again, this good faith should be continued and stressed in this matter. As recorded in Hansard at page 9009, I moved another motion requesting the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson), to do something urgently before it was too late, and as can be expected, my motion was once again rejected.
On November 24, 1975, I outlined once more the real situation in that industry in Canada. As usual the government answered that it was taking the matter into serious consideration. And I want to quote the words used by the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of industry, trade and commerce, a Liberal member sitting opposite me, and I quote:
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to note that while this sectorial strategy applied only to the leather footwear and tanning industries in the beginning, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is now considering extending its advantages to the rubber footwear subsector. This action follows the annulment, on August 28 of this year, of the general preferential tariff for rubber footwear and the reinstatement of the most favoured nation 20 per cent tariff.
As the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce stated on November 20 of this year, the government will continue to examine periodically the status of the footwear industry and to determine if other action is required in the future.

June 16, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
I therefore congratulate the hon. member for the interest that he has shown in this important industry. Moreover, as other members also said during the Liberal party caucus, we should continue to review regularly the situation of the footwear industry in Canada.
And I quite agree with those remarks, as I said earlier. I believe that if the Liberal caucus enforced more strictly the anti-inflation legislation which was introduced at the beginning of the anti-inflation program, we should have gone further and therefore should have been more efficient. Considering the situation is getting worse, I suggest we should precisely repeal this Anti-Inflation Act.
An inquiry was set up, and special reports on footwear are now before the House, dated February 24, 1972, June 29, 1973, December 21, 1973 respectively and so on. In 1971, the Anti-dumping tribunal set up an inquiry on footwear and when the report was made public in 1973, special measures were taken. What has happened? Let us look at today's situation. Between 1968 and 1975, the share of the Canadian market held by imports has increased from 38.3 to 50 per cent. If we compare the figures of 1976 and 1977 for the month of January, imports have increased by 47 per cent in these areas.
From 1975 to 1976 alone South Korea raised its shoe exports to Canada by 119.2 per cent. These are official figures recently released by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. For Greece, the raise was 137.6 per cent, for Taiwan, 84.9 per cent. The share of the Canadian market in 1977 was 32 per cent. We started with 58 per cent in 1970 and we went down to 32 per cent in 1977. And then we would like to protect the jobs of people who work and try to be more efficient in the shoe manufacturing industry. Many industries operate now at 65 and 70 per cent of their capacity. I have consulted with great care the briefs which have been presented recently to the Anti-dumping Tribunal by the Shoe Manufacturers' Association and other briefs from companies of my riding. The unions involved have presented a very consistent and very well structured memorandum to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) in January this year about this question. And now, Mr. Speaker, a well established company which has worked for 60 years in our area, Duchesse Shoe, closed its plant ten days ago. H. H. Brown Shoe Co. (Canada) Ltd., from Richmond, which had nearly 800 employees now employs about 650. Since its inception in 1953 this company was a very sound business until 1974. Since then, its sales are constantly going down, with 225,000 fewer pairs of shoes each year, a situation which brings more unemployment. Orders are at their lowest level for a seven-day cutting period while at the same time last year this period was of 27 days and so on.
In Acton Vale for example Acton Shoe Co. Limited reduced the number of its employees from 240 to 190 these last few months. In Sherbrooke, in the riding of my hon. friend and colleague, the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier), who spoke to the House not long ago-and I commend him for trying to smarten up the government-Igloo Felt closed its doors at the beginning of May and locked out, very unwillingly, 80 of its employees. I could carry on like this for hours, Mr. Speaker. What can I say to these people? Things are bad, it is true, no questions about that. I can not even tell them that

everything is going wrong, everybody knows it. But what can we do to improve things? I do not believe we should accept being swamped under imports in Canada just to maintain good business relations with other countries. Mr. Speaker, what those people in the shoe industry want is a decent job that would allow them to consider the future with serenity. I am speaking about workers who want to succeed in their business and who want to live with optimism.
Things were a little better in 1973 because the government was more attentive, it was a minority government and at that time the situation was better. It was not ideal but we could live with it. We had a minority government and it was very effective. I think it was the only time where they had a specific action program about that issue. The results were not all good but they were encouraging nonetheless. In 1974 we dropped back to the same point, especially since the anti-dumping legislation was adopted, and in the last six or twelve months it has been horrible, it is simply discouraging.
I believe the government should consider a more effective and immediate control on imports, not next year or in two years but right now.
The government should consider that issue so essential in my riding and in the surrounding area.
The government does not seem to see it that way, but I still believe is is better to feed our own children rather than the others and it is better to provide work for Canadians and help them keep their jobs rather than for friends we do not know; I mean the "anonymous importers" who are making money by the bagful-they do not even know what to do with it- through exploitation of the Canadian workers.
I do not have anything against developing countries like Taiwan, Korea or China, I do not have anything against those developing countries, but I think we should think more positively, think about our own people first. We must, as soon as possible, start an intensive campaign in Canada to provide incentives for Canadians to buy in the country. I know Canadians, especially Quebecers. They will do so, Mr. Speaker, and Canadian industries will have a better market and future in Canada.
In concluding, with your permission I would like to quote the evidence submitted by H. H. Brown Shoe Canada Ltd., from Richmond, to the anti-dumping tribunal, which is a good summary of the thinking of all the shoe industry, of all the workers in this industry and which illustrates my opinion on this situation. I hope you will excuse my English, I am not all that bilingual. The report is in English. It was submitted by H. H. Brown Shoe Canada Ltd. where everybody is perfectly bilingual. But since it was submitted in Toronto, it was drafted in English and I respect the other official language of the country.
My name is Claude Brouillette, executive vice-president of the H. H. Brown Shoe Co. (Canada) Ltd., of Richmond, Quebec.

We are a manufacturer of men's shoes, work boots, dress shoes, cowboy boots and skates.
Our daily production which was 7,000 pairs in 1973 and 1974, has presently dropped to 5,500 pairs, a drop of 22 per cent.
In 1973, we had 769 employees, whereas in 1977 we now have 656 employees, a drop of 113 employees.
A lot of these employees had been loyal employees working for our company for many years.
We are the principal employer in Richmond and have always had peaceful, pleasant labour relations.
Our company has enjoyed a successful operation, since it started in 1953 up until 1974. Since then we have lost 225,000 pairs a year.
There is no doubt that the sales we lost are due to imports coming mainly from South Korea, Taiwan, Poland, United States, Czechoslovakia, Romania and Brazil. These goods are the exact copy of our shoes, as I will demonstrate later on and are offered to our customers at prices 30 per cent below our quotations.
The situation is one of urgency and action must be taken at once. A submission that was presented to your tribunal, suggests that a committee be formed. I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that by the time the committee is formed, there will not be enough manufacturers left to form a committee.
Our designer has just spent three weeks in Europe to collect new ideas on styling, lasts, colours, etc. He also attends most of the shoe shows in Europe and America.
Our equipment and buildings are as up to date, if not better, as any of our overseas competitors.
Even if we consider the many styles and mixed sizes that we have to deal with every day, the constant loss of production during the last years, the loss to the imports in volume numbers creating a large increase in short runs, having to operate at 65 per cent of our capacity, our productivity is better than any of our operations in U.S.A. and also of any men's shoe manufacturer in America that I know.
What else can we do?
Our company is 25 years old and it is an established, respected member of the shoe industry of Canada.
We believe we have made every effort to compete with imports but without a market we cannot survive.
We want to keep supplying our customers with merchandise backed up with quality, comfort and delivery.
Mr. Chairman, we can survive only if we are provided with a decent share of the market.

Mr. Speaker, I say it again, it is urgent. One needs only read carefully the submissions I read, these and others, to know it is urgent. The fate of thousands of families and workers is in the hands of the present government. Will it deceive them once again? 1 hope, like one government member said the other night in answer to a question I asked on the shoe situation, that the Liberal caucus will consider that question. For me, I shall return to it later so that something can be done and that shoe workers can be satisfied with an economy and a trade that expand instead of shrinking. That trade must expand above all for the benefit of Canadian workers and manufacturers. To conclude, I would ask the government to abolish as soon as possible, if it is still possible in a reasonable delay so as not to create too many problems, this Anti-Inflation Act which, in my opinion, has not got to the core of the problem, that is those who really profit by inflation in the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an objection by a number of members to the passage of this bill. The parliament of Canada is being asked to water down the stock by increasing the number of shares. This company deals primarily in the public utilities field. It has a monopoly. It should be paying attention to the needs of its subscribers and the Canadian public, as well as giving some protection to the shareholders who are now involved in the ownership of Bell Canada.
Bell Canada operates in a vacuum. This may now be changing slightly. For many years the Canadian Transport Commission was the only regulatory body, other than parliament, that had any control over that company. It has recently been controlled to some degree by the CRTC. The CRTC is asking a number of questions that were never asked before on behalf of subscribers.
It is interesting to read in various articles the two different aspects of the problem we face. The CRTC had a hearing in northern Canada in March of this year, as reported in the Citizen. It was indicated at those hearings that Bell was applying for a general rate increase, the fourth in four years. They apply for one every year. This increase would have added $172 million to its annual revenue. Last year Bell took in $1.9 billion. The article states that the Inuit Association in northern Quebec has been frustrated waiting for approval from Bell to set up Taquamiut Napingat, their telephone exchange, for two years in order to provide telephone service to the residents in that area.
The CRTC has given some consideration to the public. No longer are they satisfied with the 20 cent pay telephone charge. They have given Bell six months to revert to providing ten-cent service to the public. The employees are unhappy, as are the subscribers. This government gives that company immense assistance in the satellite program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed this debate as it has meandered through the pages of Hansard. It is an interesting debate, indeed. I read with some interest the speech made by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) when introducing the bill for debate in this House. He moved that the bill be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. Like that hon. member, I wish to make a declaration with regard to shareholders.
At one time I owned some shares in Bell Canada. They treated me reasonably well during the period I held them. Because of the policies of this government the whole market
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
was affected somehow or another. Those shares suffered just a wee bit in terms of value. Last November, because I am a member of the House of Commons, I sold all the shares that 1 own. I decided to invest in Canada, and I invested in Canada Savings Bonds. I wanted to make that declaration because the hon. member for Scarborough East made a similar declaration. The hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) also made a declaration when he spoke.
There has been a rather interesting course of events. The debate began on May 27, 1977, when the hon. member for Scarborough East outlined the general provisions of the bill. His outline of the bill was satisfactory. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) also spoke in the debate on May 27 and advanced his point of view. The debate carried on. It seems to have gone on and on.
It is interesting to note that in a debate like this on March 10, 1977, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), and the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) made a speech. I think that was on the main motion. On June 2 the hon. member for Timiskaming began a speech on the motion for a six months' hoist. That is the second speech which he finished just a few minutes ago when Your Honour called him to order because his time had expired. We have had in this House a long list of NDP speeches attacking Bell Canada. As far as I am concerned, the NDP can attack whomever they like-and I do not stand particularly as an advocate for Bell Canada.
The problem with this bill is that it is highly technical. It involves an expansion of the capital stock of the company. It involves some changes in the financial provisions of the company's charter. The changes would not affect the regulatory aspects of the company. I understand the company would continue to be regulated in the same way as the British Columbia Telephone Company. This bill would give them similar powers to those granted to the British Columbia Telephone Company about two years ago.
The company says they need some improvements in terms of their financial flexibility, their powers to issue capital stock without CRTC approval. That is something that exercises my friends to the left because they are very much concerned about any move in this country to do away with the regulation of anything. If you turn over a stone somewhere and you find a member of the New Democratic Party, you will find him clutching to his breast a package of orders in council. They love orders in council. They think regulations are marvellous. Their philosophical bent is regulation of everything. However, we are all subject to redemption, and the Good Lord is prepared to forgive almost everything in all of us, even members of the NDP from time to time. I do not deny them their philosophy. Regulation by an extension of the tentacles of government into business is part of their philosophy. We respect them for that, even though from time to time we may disagree with them. They are entitled to it, and we are entitled to make a judgment on it. I know they would not deny us that privilege.
June 16, 1977

As I understand these highly technical provisions, an attempt is being made to incorporate some sections into the statute law affecting Bell Canada that are involved in other Canadian corporations. As I understand it, the intention of the bill is to authorize the company to alter its objectives, powers and share capital by applying to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott), and there is some attempt-1 do not know whether it is a good attempt or not, and I do not know how we could find that out on second reading-to provide, by way of a negative resolution, the cancellation of the powers by either House of parliament. That, by the way, is provided, I understand, in the Telesat Canada Act. It is not a new procedure.
The reason I rose to take part in the debate is that I have followed it since the outset. I do not agree with all the arguments that have been advanced by those who oppose the bill. I do not think Bell Canada is saintly, by any means. I do not stand as an advocate of Bell Canada, but I am very much concerned that the affairs of the company, which says it has problems, be tested in the House of Commons in a debate on second reading. There is now an amendment for a six months' hoist. I do not know how any member of the House can examine the officials of Bell Canada to see whether or not they need those powers, whether they need the changes that they ask for, unless this bill goes to committee.
Because of its nature, Bell Canada, being incorporated by public act, comes to this parliament to ask for a change in certain things. Once that has happened with a company providing a public service, whether that service is good or bad- that can be examined, too, in context of the bill-I think this parliament owes that company some attention, whether it is Bell Canada or any other public utility that is incorporated, or any company or organization providing a service subject to the jurisdiction of parliament. We owe it not just attention in a repetitive way-and unfortunately that has been the thrust of the debate, a repetition of the same old arguments-but a minute examination of the officers of the company, the requirements of the company, the changes they propose, their effect upon shareholders and subscribers, and a whole host of other things. In other words, this is not an ordinary private bill, it is a bill involving a company that, for better or worse, provides a service to a number of Canadians.
I think we ought to move reasonably quickly to send this bill to the committee. I am satisfied that if Bell Canada were found wanting in the ways that have been described with eloquence by the hon. member for Timiskaming and other members who spoke in the debate, there is no member of the House who would be prepared to grant them those powers. Bell Canada may not get them anyway because of some of the provisions which, upon examination, may be found wanting in terms of the ability of Bell Canada to make a case when they come before the committee.
However, I think it is fair and reasonable for some assumptions to be made. One of those assumptions is that Bell
Bell Canada
Canada's presently authorized maximum capital of $1.7 billion is expected to be exhausted in 1978. That is an assertion by the company. If that assertion is wrong, if the company has misled parliament with respect to the bill, then they ought to be pitched out of court. But I say to you that they have to get to the courtroom before we can know. That is the real issue, and that is the reason I was moved to take part in the debate.
I have sat here through all but one of the speeches that have been made, and I would not say it is an unreasonable use of the rules of the House to carry on the debate. But I think there comes a time in matters of such a technical nature when the debate should end and we should get the issue into the commitee where witnesses can be called, technical people from within government can be called, perhaps people from CRTC, and a host of others can be called and the question looked at. I base that on the assertion that has been made by the company that they require it. They would be fools to come to parliamnt if they didn't require it. Let us find out if they are fools or not, and let us find out in the committee what the facts are. We cannot do so on second reading; we can merely assert certain things. That is one of the difficulties with second reading debate.
Therefore, I hope that for the purposes of that examination, the NDP will reconsider its motion to hoist the bill for six months and will allow the officials of the company and parliamentarians to examine the bill to see if the case can be made but if parliament does not give them a chance to present it, we would be denying the company their day in court. They cannot get their day in court on second reading debate. They get their day in court in a committee of the House. I will conclude by saying that I think we should allow them to get to the committee where this parliament should take this bill apart and demand all the information. It has more power than any other group to demand information, because it can deny ultimate approval if the information is not forthcoming. We should make the company prove their case and we should not use this amendment procedure, having regard to the purposes of the company which were established by statute of parliament and should be regulated reasonably by parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that not one of my colleagues was shocked by the fact that I supported a motion of an NDP member to postpone the study of this important bill for six months. I did so quite freely and with a full awareness of my responsibilities because I consider communications an extremely important area. I have no animosity towards Bell Canada, but I would not want it to become a monopoly in the field of communications in our country. First, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about a famous Canadian who gave man this great invention that we call the telephone.
Mr. Speaker, I believe we do not say as often as we should all that Canada has given man through its citizens. When we travel throughout the world, when we are in European or

June 16, 1977
Bell Canada
Asian countries, we have to place our calls 24, 48 and even 60 hours in advance to communicate with our families in Canada, while in our own country, we have the advantage of being able to place our calls very quickly. This is a great service, but it is also very costly.
If Graham Bell had waited, as certain people want us to do today when we suggest something new in any area, in the area of finance, for instance, as I have done very often, he would have been told, like certain members tell us: Has this been done elsewhere?
Mr. Speaker, if Graham Bell had waited to invent the telephone, if he had wondered if it had been done elsewhere, if the Chinese had done it or if the Russians had done it, today, in 1977, man could still be waiting for this great means of communication. Mr. Speaker, as I have said already, we must not ape others, we must not wait for others to try something so that we may imitate them. Canadians can innovate in any area. Graham Bell understood this. I want to recall his memory because he was a great Canadian who rendered a great service, not only to Canada, but to the whole world. Today, we are studying Bill S-2 which concerns communications.
And in the communications field in Canada we almost have a monopoly in the hands of Bell Canada. We have cooperatives throughout the country who operate and offer services in areas where Bell Canada is not able to make profits. I know what I am talking about, Mr. Speaker. I have spent 20 years in the communication field. I was living in a settlement area where there was no telephone service. When we asked the Bell Company which was located 30 miles from our place in the city of Quebec to give us communication and telephone services they answered they could not do it because it was not profitable for them.
However, we had in the vicinity a company called Quebec Telephone owned by a great Liberal senator who has been in the Senate for several years, Mr. Jules Brillant, who made every effort to develop in the area a telephone service to meet the needs of the population. At that time, Quebec Telephone had jurisdiction over the area but it did not have the financial means to meet the needs of the population. So we called upon Bell Telephone, but they did not agree to give us a service for which we were ready to pay saying it would not be profitable.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we decided to organize with the cooperation of people of goodwill what we called a cooperative network. We founded telephone cooperatives based on the Cooperative unions legislation of the province of Quebec and we succeeded in offering to the people of the areas not served by Bell Telephone the communications means they needed. We had, in the circumstances, to buy all the equipment needed from the Northern Electric Company, a subsidiary of Bell Telephone, and to accept the price set by them as they had no competition. Then, the only company that could supply the equipment for those new communication services to those Cooperative unions was the Northern Electric, a subsidiary of Bell Telephone. Mr. Speaker, later when it became profitable we saw that monopoly establish itself in those areas and today,

like in the rest of the country, the telephone service there is very costly because of the lack of competition.
I am a member of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services and I am sometimes shocked by the fact that the Canadian Parliament has to give in to the will of Bell Canada to ensure the members of the House of Commons are granted a vital service that enables them to serve the Canadian people, be it from Ottawa, or from the office that each of them maintains in his riding. We feel as if we were caught in a vise. We have become the slaves of a monopoly in communications. And today, through Bill S-2 the House is again being asked to make more concessions and grant Bell Canada additional powers.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot do this inconsiderately. We must come to a halt and consider objectively whether the demands contained in Bill S-2 are really grounded. This is one of the reasons that compelled me to back the motion presented by the member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), without considering which party we respectively belong to. For me, it does not matter, Mr. Speaker. What matters are our duties as members of this House. I would have done the very same thing for a Liberal member such as the one sitting in front of me, the member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron), or even the one who represents the official opposition as parliamentary leader in the House. I would have done it the same way. Why so? Because I look at our responsibilities not from a partisan's angle, but from the viewpoint of the interests that have to be served by this Parliament which is accountable to the Canadian people for a service given to this very people and to prevent a further growth of this monopoly in communications.
Mr. Speaker, let us read the explanatory notes to that bill:
The said Company shall have power to manufacture telephones and other apparatus connected therewith, and their appurtenances and other instruments, used in connection with the business of a telegraph or telephone company, and also such other electrical instruments and plant as the said Company may deem advisable, and to purchase, sell or lease the same and rights relating thereto, and to build, establish, construct, purchase, acquire or lease, and maintain and operate, or sell or let any line or lines for the transmission of messages by telephone, in Canada or elsewhere, and to make connection, for the purpose of telephone business, with the line or lines of any telegraph or telephone company in Canada or elsewhere, and to aid or advance money to build or work any such line to be used for telephone purposes:
This occurred in 1949, Mr. Speaker. We are now in 1977. Parliament has been unable to progress in this respect. I know it, Mr. Speaker, and I can say so very strongly, although at a certain time Mr. Louis-Philippe Lacroix, the former member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine in the Quebec National Assembly, made false statements against yours truly while he was acting as the manager of a telephone co-operative.
Mr. Speaker, 1 can prove on the basis of my past experience that the area of communications is highly profitable. Because I should like to prove it, I suggest that we should not, without serious reason, grant new privileges to a company which is something of a monopoly, judging from official data. I still have all these documents. They were given to me as a gift by a grateful board of directors as a reward for the great services I have rendered the Canadian people. Not only do I have them,
June 16, 1977

but I have them here, in my Ottawa office, where I keep them as a precious heirloom.
Mr. Speaker, I will give an example to the House to show that the field of communications is profitable and that we must not extend to Bell Canada new privileges which will enable it to create an even more powerful monopoly.

This is a major Canadian corporation supplying important public services as a public utility, and parliament obliges it to come to this House to seek changes in its charter and its capitalization. The only way this corporation, in contrast to others, can make these changes is to come here. Therefore the procedures we put it through should have relevance to the public interest of the company.
This is the point I am trying to raise because I am going to ask you, as guardian of our interests as private members, if there is a way we could seek a change in the rules. This company must come through a private member. I sponsored the bill in the House. It must be a private bill debated in private members' hour, which in the normal course arises on Thursdays every two weeks. If there is another private bill it arises once every four weeks, and if there are three, it is every six weeks, and many of those occasions do not take place for reasons with which we are all familiar.

That means we oblige the corporation to enter into a procedure which may have no result, with no decision, and in fact there may well be no decision in this session or in the next session. Indeed, there may be no decision at all because this bill may not proceed beyond second reading stage. The company may never get its day in court. I would therefore like to ask whether we are not making a farce of our own institution by the way we proceed.
I should like to suggest that we make some proceeding available through either Standing Order 75A or 75B to cover circumstances such as these.
This whole procedure is divorced from the government; it is divorced from the minister. Are we to be helpless and make a farce of our own institution because we can be held up, session after session after session, when a major corporation is told to come here and we can offer it no result? Mr. Speaker, I think you are the guardian of our interests as private members. We cannot turn to the House leader or to the government; we turn to ourselves. I ask if you, Mr. Speaker, as our guardian, could refer this matter of private bills, and the procedure for dealing with them, to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I suggest specifically that the chairman of the committee should have the right to seek the kind of all-party, or majority party agreement, which will enable us to consider this kind of bill under a time allocation.
Let us give ourselves some rules which will prevent our running into these impasses, which surely are an affront to the nearly quarter of a million Canadians who own this company, and to the millions of Canadians served by it. We shall deny those Canadians proper service if we deny this company the financing and corporate strength it needs to do its job. We make a farce of ourselves and I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, to do something about it.

CONFLICT OF INTEREST-ACTIVITIES OF SENATOR DAVEY RESPECTING CERTAIN COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to pursue the question I took up with the government House leader in his capacity as Actisig Prime Minister last Monday, when I questioned the role of Senator Keith Davey, if in fact he had any role, in other enterprises in addition to the one which received so much prominence in the Toronto Sun, for which he used to be an eminent correspondent, that is to say, Blue Water Racing Associates Ltd.
I am interested in this matter for several reasons, Mr. Speaker. I was less than impressed with the government House leader's response which he made on the subject of conflict of interest a few days earlier, I think on June 10, when he referred to a green paper and made mention of a bill which was coming along on the subject of conflict of interest.
Over the years there has been a gradual improvement, 1 suggest, in the general atmosphere. One of the most important steps was taken by a former prime minister, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), when he discouraged, if not outrightly prohibited, as I recall, cabinet ministers from holding directorships or taking part in business while they were members of cabinet.
To some extent the Canadian people are now convinced that the Senate is nothing more than a repository for people using their substantial Senate salaries to provide themselves with a secure income which allows them to participate in commercial ventures for their own benefit. When they are not doing that, they are perceived to be paid organizers, in effect, for their parties. This is not being fair to most of the Senators, but even if only a few of them are actually carrying on this type of
Adjournment Debate
lifestyle, it does reflect badly on the many conscientious Senators who are doing the best they can to discharge their responsibilities.
I became very interested in a company called Hydroculture Luwasa Limited which participates in the esoteric business of growing plants by the addition of nutrients, a very interesting process. When I noted that this particular company, which was incorporated on July 12, 1975, under the corporate name of Hydoculture Luwasa Limited, had as a director none other than Senator Keith Davey, I asked myself what in the world would he be doing, involved in an enterprise like this? Then I began to think: "Well, there is enough greenery and foliage around some of these government offices to make a Tarzan movie", and one almost expect to see a cheetah peeking through some of the foliage in some government buildings. So I obtained a list of the directors and officers. 1 should like the government Efouse leader to take it as notice to supplement some of the information which I have.
I am interested to know, for example, whether the Senator is still a director in this company. Is he now a shareholder? I want to know to what extent the company does business with the federal government or Crown agencies. 1 should like to know some other information to supplement my own. I should like to know, if it is relevant, why this company was negotiating to sell itself to another company in a highly regulated but unrelated field, Canadian Cable Systems, Ltd. Senator Davey has been mentioned in other matters, for example, Blue Water Racing Associates Ltd.
The whole situation seems to be something which is not in the best interests of the parliamentary system. I do not want to sound sanctimonious about this, but at this particular point in time it seems unfortunate that a man such as Senator Davey, who is a key campaign adviser, a political strategist in government and a man of prominence, is perceived to be in a position such as was indicated by the Toronto Sun. That newspaper said that his assistance in licensing involves setting up meetings with federal and provincial officials in charge of licensing. That is worrisome. It is very interesting why he would receive a 50 per cent equity in a company in which he did not invest any cash, if there was not some valuable emphasis placed on the type of assistance he would be providing in this regard.
When we take this and equate it with the rather interesting situation involved in this other company, there may or may not be a pattern emerging here. I would like the government, in connection with its study of conflicts of interest, green papers, and proposed legislation, to consider this particular item. In due course 1 would appreciate having a bit more information on Senator Davey's equity, his present position in Hydroculture Luwasa Canada, Ltd., and also whether there may be other shareholders, who are in a prominent position in the government service or elsewhere, who ought to reconsider their positions with respect to the type of business this company is doing or proposes to do with the Government of Canada.

Senator Davey has had discussion with Mr. S. B. Pratt, the former chief supervisor, who retired in June of 1975, and the present chief supervisor, Mr. B. He has contacted the Department of Agriculture, but the senior people whom I named in my earlier answer indicated that no
Adjournment Debate

As to the price paid for the senator's interest in that company, perhaps that is a matter for further questions if the hon. member wishes to pursue this. It is getting a little deep for this type of questioning.

As to doing business with the government, this is becoming a massive problem. It is almost impossible these days to avoid running into regulations, federal, provincial or municipal. The question becomes whether, in the face of various regulations of Crown agencies and departments, members of parliament and Senators are expected to have no business interests whatsoever.
I am not making any comment on the validity or otherwise of that. I am simply saying that our regulated lifestyle is becoming such that it is hard to avoid bumping into some level of government somewhere.
1 remember very recently in the case of the department of which 1 was parliamentary secretary that that department purchased an airplane for the use of the RCMP from a member of parliament. That can be said to be doing business with the Government of Canada. I think we could get to the stage where we could find some fault or issue of morality in that type of transaction, and then all of us will have to live in some kind of state that is not natural to the human being.
Again, I do not indicate that the greatest of care is not necessary. It certainly is, and I am not commenting on the issue raised by the hon. member. I am simply trying to answer some of the observations made with respect to conflicts of interest, in some measure because I used to be the chairman of the committee responsible for the green paper. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that I should like to talk about the resolution in four perspectives, the first with regard to the program itself.
Obviously the best way to consider the program is to cast it against the backdrop of the experience that Canada was going through in the late summer and fall of 1975 when it was first put into effect. While at that time some of the costs, which over the previous two years we and other world economies had been absorbing, had peaked and we had seen some reductions, the atmosphere in Canada was one of expectation of ever-increasing inflation. There were those who were seeking price or income increases not just to recover the percentage increase in the consumer price index in the previous period but in many cases to anticipate even further rates of inflation which they expected to come. It was an atmosphere of a certain kind of envy, of competitive claims based as much on comparison with the percentage increases of others as on actual need.
The inflation rate at that time was 10.6 per cent, the rate of settlements in the first year was an annual rate of 20 per cent, and unit labour costs were at 15.2 per cent. The initial claims of collective bargaining in the last weeks of September and in early October were in the skyrocketing 50 to 60 per cent range. The consensus discussions which had been carried on in the previous winter and spring by my predecessor and other colleagues with some of the major economic decision makers in Canada had disclosed the difficulty of obtaining voluntary agreements to restrain against inflationary increases.
The major groups which had been consulted evidenced a substantial distrust of voluntary restraint and, in particular, a certain suspicion that even if they restrained themselves some of the other major groups might not agree.
Under the circumstances it was clear that only a mandatory program imposing legal restraints on the great economic powers-large firms, major union groups, the public sector, professionals-could bring about a restraint on the frenzy of the inflationary spiral then under way.
I think it is fair to say that the program has succeeded in reducing the spiral of expectation. Early in the program it was
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
clear that certain commodities such as food, energy or imported goods could not be effectively controlled. The United States had attempted to control food in their program and it only brought about higher prices and diminution of supply.
It was recognized that certain economic factors, such as the change in the external value of the Canadian dollar, or interest rates, could not be controlled. Subject to these limitations we set out to restrain the powerful in the community, and it can be said that the program succeeded in doing that. The rate of inflation has come down from 10.6 per cent to 6.2 per cent in October, 1976. Using the same index-not switching the index as the hon. member might-it came down to a current rate of 7.6 per cent. Aided by reductions in food prices at first, and the food price reduction was important and significant, the rate of price increase has come down.
It is fair to point out in connection with food prices that 60 per cent of the cost of the food going through to the consumer at the retail level is made up of the cost of processing, packaging, transporting and retailing, and the anti-inflation program was effective in restraining those cost increases so that the real cuts in prices were passed along to consumers. Food prices have risen again, principally because of shortages arising from crop conditions abroad, but we have some reason to hope that, with favourable conditions in Canada, some of these increases will be reversed.
The critical element to be understood, both in relation to the program and in relation to inflation generally in the years to come, is that not all elements of the cost-price chain can be subjected to control. Real cost increases in some commodities are unavoidable, commodities such as energy, or food when it is in short supply, or, as the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) mentioned this afternoon, imports, these being all cases in which the community has no choice but to meet the higher costs. But we can modify our own wage and salary increases, or modify, in the case of the business sector, the additional claims for profit.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext: But that does not apply to the government.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977

The program has not meant hardship for the working man; I think this is an important element to underline. For example, average wage rates increased in 1976 at the rate of 10 per cent, and the consumer price index through that year increased at a rate of 6.5 per cent; therefore, there were real increases for the average working man of between 3 per cent and 4 per cent in the year. Hence the moderation in the cost of living has yielded real benefits for the community as a whole. But it must be understood at the same time that some factors, for example the increase in food prices, will mean additional costs for the community. I do not think we can undertake to assure the community that they can enjoy all the benefits of a drop in costs, for example the drop in food prices to a certain extent, and at the same time be cushioned against any increases which might take place. There are going to be flows and ebbs in
June 16, 1977

take-home pay. But the critical thing is to maintain a reasonable balance over a period of time with respect to costs people will have to meet.
I now come to the question of prices. There has been a significant drop in the rate of increase, particularly on the non-food side of price increases. For many firms market conditions have operated to hold down price increases, but for other firms the restraint on profits and profit margins has provided a check.
Close to 300 firms must notify the Anti-Inflation Board in advance of their intention to increase prices, and the results of this process give one indication of future consumer price performance. In 1976, for example, pre-notified price increases averaged 6.8 per cent. In the first four months of this year the rate was 4.1 per cent, and in April alone it was down to 3 per cent. The fact is, we are bringing costs under control in Canada.
Unit labour costs, as I mentioned before, increased in 1975 at an annual rate of 15.2 per cent. First year wage settlements, after increasing by 20 per cent in 1975, had dropped progressively, to 9.9 per cent by the fourth quarter of last year, and to 8.8 per cent by the first quarter of 1977. Month by month the compensation plans filed with the Anti-Inflation Board have moved closer to the anti-inflation guidelines, an indication of acceptance and compliance by workers and employers.
The strike record in Canada now is vastly better than it has been in recent years. In January and February of this current year, the number of man-days lost nationally through labour disputes was 70 per cent below the number lost in the same months of 1976. More agreements are being signed by employers and unions without the need of arbitration or mediation. I think some credit is due to both sides of the bargaining table for the sense of responsibility which has activated the trends I indicated in those figures.
One industry in particular deserves credit, the construction industry. I refer now to an article which appeared in the Financial Times under the byline of Mr. Clayton Sinclair, who refers to the fact that in the construction industry there has been a dramatic drop in wage increases. Fie wrote, and I quote:
Construction industry wage settlements, for years the bane of inflation fighters, are rolling in this spring at levels so low management and even some government officials find them hard to believe ...
This year, instead of getting 17 per cent pay increases as they did back in 1975, 200,000 tradesmen and labourers who have been negotiating in Ontario and farther west since early April will wind up, according to reports from the Anti-Inflation Board, with something closer to 7 per cent-fringe benefits included.
More than 250 contracts covering the bulk of organized construction workers in British Columbia, Ontario and on the Prairies opened this spring. By last week close to 85 per cent had either been renewed or were awaiting ratification.
He gave some examples, and perhaps I may be forgiven for being parochial in quoting the following example:
Ontario's workforce is now settling for increases worth 90 cents an hour or close to 7 per cent after signing two years ago for raises worth $3.50 an hour. In Toronto, plumbers who were getting $13.66 hourly settled for $14.56 when their agreement was signed last month.
Anti-Inflation Act
Clearly, there is evidence of a new sense of responsibility on both sides of the bargaining table, a responsibility which has been effective as well at the national leadership level, both on the business and labour side.
I have mentioned some of the immediate benefits of a lower rate of inflation in Canada and the impact on our industrial costs.
One of the points which has been made, validly I think, is this: while controls have provided a temporary relief, if they are to be of long-lasting value they have to bring about some substantial change, perhaps of a structural nature, perhaps of a psychological nature. In any event, there must be some change in the approach which all those involved in economic decision-making bring to bear on the decisions they have to take.
I suppose the question is, what was changed as a result of the 20-month experience? I think the leaders of the big battalions at least have learned something from the experience.
I think they have learned, for example, that notwithstanding their claims as economic decision-makers to be able to make some decisions and pass them freely on to the public, the public remains very skeptical. Indeed, the fact that many ordinary Canadians have a great deal of hesitation about the government taking off controls reflects their skepticism. Nor do they have enormous confidence that their leaders decisions will necessarily be in the best interests of all.
We have had in Canada the phenomenon of rising popularity of the controls program, especially on the part of those who do not now have collective power. This fact shows up in the polls, it shows up in the personal contacts I have, and 1 know it is showing up in the contacts my colleagues have had as well in their own constituencies and throughout the country.

I would point out to the hon. member that he had one and he was wiped out.
Let us turn, now, to the next question, the question of decontrol itself. There are really two principal choices involved. The first is the immediate and simultaneous with-

drawal of controls, the so-called "lights out" method set out in the green paper. The second choice is the phased withdrawal of controls. That choice, called the third option, is outlined in some detail in the green paper.
The government favours the second approach, for two reasons. First, it avoids the risk of a sudden and simultaneous outburst of price and income increases, or at least it minimizes that risk to the extent it can be minimized-what the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) called the "springback"-when controls are lifted as people seek to recover some part of their loss of income. Second, it would make for increased fairness as between different bargaining groups. If the House were to accept this motion on Monday evening, the situation would be that controls would have been applied to those who had voluntarily complied with the guidelines and stayed within them, while those who had held out against controls, those who had not supported the program, those who had delayed collective bargaining or failed to enter into an agreement, would benefit by the fact that controls had come off.
One thing is clear. Whatever method is chosen for decontrol, we would invite both unfairness and a wage-price explosion unless we deal with the problem of unamended agreements under the anti-inflation program. Let me explain. In the course of the program many collective agreements have been reached at rates of interest substantially higher than the anti-inflation guidelines. Some of these increases have been rolled back by recommendation of the Anti-Inflation Board. Others have been reduced by order of the Administrator. As long as the controls are in force, compensation is being paid to employees at the rates established by the Board or by the Administrator. However, many of the contracts have not actually been rewritten to reflect rulings by the Anti-Inflation Board or by the Administrator, and still provide for the rates originally negotiated.
There is some uncertainty about the legal situation once the controls are removed and the agreements cease to be subject to mandatory restraint. Employees might be able to demand as a matter of right that their compensation be increased to the levels provided by the letter of unamended contracts. Employers might be legally obliged to pay the negotiated rates, in addition, employees might be able to make up their so-called past losses, that is, the difference between the negotiated rates and the allowable rates for the period during which their agreements were under controls. Obviously this situation would be highly unfair to those who have complied with the program by negotiating agreements within the guidelines in the first place or who amended their contracts to conform with the rulings. Furthermore, if these agreements were allowed to stand and if the negotiated rates were paid, the consequences for the economy could be serious.
With lights out decontrol there could be a large, immediate jump in wages, combined with big lump-sum payments immediately following the decontrols date. This could at once place severe pressure on prices and drive up inflationary expectations as other groups sought instant catch-up. Down
June 16, 1977

the road, it would cost the economy a lot of jobs. Even if a phased decontrol were adopted, pressure would mount steadily and much of the benefit of the program would be seen to be thrown away. A substantial number of large increases over time would still provide a powerful demonstration effect to other groups.
To provide for greater certainty with the approach of decontrol, the government has therefore decided to propose amendments to the Anti-Inflation Act to deem these agreements to be amended in line with the AIB recommendation or order of the Administrator. An amending bill would be introduced to deal with this. In the same way, the law will make sure that profit restraints imposed, for example, by excess revenue orders, will be effective.

The leaders of the CLC, for example, speak only for their own membership, and the congress does not purport to represent the whole of Canadian labour. Representatives of business are quick to point out that they can speak only for their own companies and that, while they are prepared to advocate restraint, they cannot be sure that others will follow. We shall be seeking further assurance as to the active advocacy of policies of restraint we can expect from these groups.
As well we are seeking from these groups a commitment to their participation in the two institutional changes we have proposed in the white paper, in the Agenda for Co-operation. We have proposed these two institutions, a consultative forum and a monitoring agency, and it is critical that they both have the support of business and labour in Canada.
Will they participate? In light of the experience with the Economic Council, will they even attend? 1 do not think we know yet. Although we have made the green paper available for their examination and study of these particular questions, we have no clear indication at the moment that they are prepared to participate in these organizations. We have put the questions to them and, if they are not prepared to participate in this kind of consultation as such, what changes or what
Anti-Inflation Act
methods would they propose to try to achieve better restraint in the post-controls period? This is obviously a role to be defined 1n consultation with the group. We have been seeking a meeting just as soon as they are ready for the purpose of talking on this question, and once we have had their reaction it will fall back on the government to make a final decision as to the date and the method of decontrol.
On the question of the forum, I should like to turn for a moment from purely Canadian sources to an international report, one that I can recommend to hon. members. It is the recent report of the secretary of the OECD entitled "Toward Full Employment and Price Stability". It is a penetrating examination of the problems of economic management in a modern economy and is prepared by a group of independent experts under the leadership of Mr. Paul McCracken, former chairman of the United States council of economic advisers. I should just like to quote briefly a section from the heart of that report:
We support the idea that governments should discuss regularly with the organizations representing business and labour the general evolution of prices and wages which should be aimed at over the coming year or so, consistant with achieving or maintaining high employment levels.
The report goes on:
Five years ago, it was understandable that representatives of business and labour might take it for granted that governments had it in their power to ensure high levels of sales and employment. They may well have felt that the warnings against the dire consequences of irresponsible behaviour on their part need not be taken seriously. All this has now changed.
I have spoken of the consultative forum. 1 will make reference only to the monitoring agency briefly because the agency and its function are fully described in the Agenda for CoOperation. Its function is to follow economic developments, to comment on specific price or wage changes which could have an adverse impact on inflation in Canada, and to comment as well on trends in the economy which would have the same direction. It would be an agency which is consistent with the free choice option which we have taken in the post-controls period. Its responsibility would be limited to requiring information from the major economic decision makers and to public reporting. It would not have responsibility for mandatory control of either prices or wages.
This is a concept that has been not unknown to us in this country in the last several years. I refer by way of comparison to the Estey commission which examined the steel industry and steel prices in Canada, or to the better known work of the food prices review commission which examined the food industry in the same context.
With respect to the consultative forum, 1 stress two of the underlying objectives. There are really two elements involved in it. There is the concept of responsibility and that of co-operation.
Responsibility assumes that the private sector will have freedom to come to decisions, but that in doing so there is the expectation that it will take into account the wider impact in the community and the longer term impact on either the union or the company in question if a reasonable balance is upset in economic decision making.
