Co-operation assumes a substantial departure from the atmosphere of adversary negotiation in the private sector or from arm's length dealing between the parties. It assumes that there will be a meeting at which the economic aspirations of each particular group can be represented, the group being either union members or shareholders. It will also be assumed that it is not inconsistent with looking after the interests of a particular group that it should meet with others in the community, and that the wider objectives of the community should be taken into account.
Both institutions which are proposed are intended to provide better information in regard to trends in the economy and an understanding of those trends, and also better communication between the major decision makers.
Finally, I turn to comments made by other members in this debate. In addition to the remarks of the hon. member for York-Simcoe we have the advantage of the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in Montreal last week end. I think it is fair to characterize their approach to this particular motion as being that we should bring about an end to controls in the form in which they exist at the present time, but that they should be re-established, albeit for a brief period, in some other form.
I think the shortcomings that 1 find with that proposal would be both administrative and legal. There is also some question whether the proposed reinstallation of controls, as set out by the Leader of the Opposition last weekend, could be effective.
One of the elements that I did find rather puzzling was the notion in both statements that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should become the recipient of these activities. Indeed, the hon. member for York-Simcoe said this afternoon that some of the activities of that department would have to be discontinued so that the staff in the department could attend to the monitoring procedures which are now carried out by the Anti-Inflation Board.

They want to put in place some kind of vague, ill-defined system of controls for six or 12 months for which there may not be any legislative base. May I suggest to hon. members that that kind of invitation should be turned down, and I look forward to your support in voting with me on Monday night against the proposition which has been put forward.

Ours may not be perfect and we admit that, but at least it works and has been accepted by Canadians. At least the NDP offered a basic definition of principles typical of that party, although we do not share them. 1 was puzzled by the idea of a national incomes policy because, as I understand the meaning of the phrase, it would mean interfering with the collective bargaining process and then having to come back to something similar to what is already in place now. In essence it would mean that by June 30 we should do away with something that has proven itself and which we are trying to improve-and replace it with something that requires a fundamental change in our economic and social structures, structures that we are far from having reached, as the hon. member for Halifax said. The alternative put forward by the NDP was a nice exercise in theoretical analysis of what could be done in outer space, but it is something that cannot be done in Canada in 1977 A.D.
I am tempted to think that if the NDP were not so strongly supported by strong organizations they would freely and happily support the policy we now have through the Anti-Inflation Board. This is really a form of economic controls and economic planning that they would otherwise be quite happy to endorse, but which they apparently cannot for reasons of their own.
I have already outlined briefly why we adopted controls and what we said in 1974. It can be claimed that controls have served Canadians well, otherwise they would not have the support of the population which the hon. member for Halifax referred to when he spoke of political convenience on our part. Instead, from our point of view, from the rough beginnings in October and November of 1975 we have come a long way in developing a consensus and acceptance of these measures across the country, when at that time it almost seemed as if we were reaching for the impossible and when we were very unpopular for doing so.
The opposition seems to forget that this government had the courage and determination needed to introduce a measure which it knew would be highly unpopular in the beginning. It was very hot in the kitchen at that time, being criticized here everyday and every weekend in the riding, but 20 months later we are reaping the benefits of that approach.
It seems to me that we should not end controls at this point. They were introduced because we had an emergency in inflation. When inflation hovers around 6 per cent or 7 per cent and is accompanied by high levels of unemployment, the emergency continues to exist as long as we have high levels of unemployment. There is therefore good reason for continuing the controls, not only until the end of 1978 but beyond that if unemployment remains high.
It begins to be quite clear that inflation at the rate we know it is standing in the way of the creation of new jobs and the reduction of unemployment. There is a link between the two- a necessity to bring down inflation in order to bring down unemployment. Anyone in this House who urges the government to do something about unemployment but who does not support its policies to bring down inflation is forgetting this
essential link in the economic conditions of the seventies which are different from the economic conditions and symptoms of previous years.
I would urge the Anti-Inflation Board to be more conscious of fees and executive salaries, however. This is an area in which we seem to have failed, at least partially, to exert the controls that have been exerted on other sectors of the population. The Anti-Inflation Board must do a better job in this area.
I also think we must have a program of income support for the low income earners. They get the short end of the stick and are more intensely affected in inflationary times. There are the groups that suffer during a prolonged period of inflation both in rural Canada and the industrial areas. An income support program would help them make ends meet.
Controls are a measure that result from a new set of economic conditions in the world, not only in Canada. We see the controls as a bridge to a new approach to the solution of economic problems. We are searching for the answers and, in doing so, have put in place this policy which will provide us with breathing space and permit us to devise the new levers we shall need to deal with a new economic order.
The Conservatives will continue to speak of our free market place, and God bless them for it! That is the kind of dinosaur approach we shall gladly leave with them. I say to them, have a good trip. So long as the Conservatives believe in the free market place they will remain in opposition.
As for the NDP, it continues to speak of a fully planned economy. We, as Liberals, believe in a flexible approach. We like to find an answer which comes between those two extremes. Though it may be difficult to find, I am confident that, given time and the opportunity, we shall find it.
The emergency which existed in late 1975 led to the introduction of this program, which has'had an impact on inflation. The emergency exists so long as we have high unemployment. How are we to bring down unemployment? We can do it, I suggest, by introducing policies which will lead to a disciplined economy, to confidence in the economy, to a stable economy, and therefore to a climate of confidence which will induce investment in the economy. That is where we differ from the Progressive Conservatives.
We believe that if we have a smoothly working system of controls we will have discipline in the economy, and that entrepreneurs will be ready to expand their operations. They will have confidence in the future of our economy and so will provide the investment we need in order to create new jobs. If we do as the Conservatives say, our future will be uncertain, for no one will know what the inflation rate will be in three months, or six months. If we adopt the kind of scheme the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) proposes, we would give the private sector the excuse not to invest and to expand this economy, an expansion we need to create new employment.

June 16, 1977

We all know the effects of inflation. They make us less competitive with other countries. Therefore inflation endangers our jobs at home and makes us less able to sell our products at home and abroad. Second, inflation shifts purchasing power from low to high income groups. That is why I spoke earlier about the necessity of income support programs, or a guaranteed income for lower income groups such as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has advocated in recent years.
If we adopted the proposal of the hon. member for York-Simcoe, within a short time the official opposition would scream about high wage settlements. They would raise hell about it. They would be the first to complain of high wage settlements. As for the NDP, if we do what they suggest, what would happen? They would scream about high profits and high prices. Mr. Speaker, the reaction would come from the other side of the House. The opposition would criticize, and within a short time would ask the government to enact corrective measures.	.
We Liberals will stand up and vote against this proposal because we want to protect unorganized workers, to protect pensioners and all those not represented by strong groups in society, those who are hardest hit and most devastatingly affected by the evils of inflation. We believe that the government's policy and program, imperfect though they may be because of shortcomings, are by far the better approach, and serve the interests of Canadians better than would the adoption of the proposal the Conservatives have put forward today for debate.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am glad the hon. member who just resumed his seat intends to vote against the motion. I would not want to be on his side, for 1 do not agree with his arguments on this important subject.
I wish to lend my support to this motion because I do not believe there is a legitimate reason for retaining controls, with the possible exception of standby controls which may be needed if something unusual happens in the economy. Any value the controls may have had initially is now exhausted. 1 myself did not feel controls should ever have been instituted, and certainly not in the present situation. We were not at war, as we were in the 1940's. In the war years controls were necessary, I feel, though experience then indicated that disparities and inequities were the result.
There are many reasons for lifting these controls. Some suspect the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government of wanting ever-increasing controls to remain part of our economic and social future. The Prime Minister's statement, in his now famous speech delivered before Christmas, 1975, to the effect that the free market is no longer operating and could not be allowed to function has been received unfavourably almost by everyone. It must have been a severe blow to the Prime Minister when the federal green paper on decontrol said, "It is the wish of most Canadians to maintain and strengthen this mixed economy with the great preponderance of economic decisions taking place within the private sector. That statement was supposed to reassure those who were
Anti-Inflation Act
afraid controls would be made permanent. Nevertheless, many in this country are growing increasingly afraid that the government will so like controls it will keep them in place indefinitely.
Again, the green paper on decontrols had this to say: "The challenges of operating a healthy and stable economy without mandatory controls must be met."
Canada is not only in serious economic difficulty but in serious political difficulty. Yesterday I noticed a newspaper report saying that Mr. Laurin, the Quebec minister in charge of Bill C-l, suggested that even if 23,000 jobs are lost in the province of Quebec, it is the risk the province may just have to take if it is to realize the broader social goals of its language bill. It shows how sincere is the desire for political independence in Quebec, and how sincerely the present government of that province is willing to pursue it.
Once more we confront the serious problem of unemployment. The headlines in yesterday's Montreal Gazette note that the jobless gap is growing wider between Quebec and the rest of the nation. One article said 274,000 people in Quebec are without a job now, as compared to 215,000 one year ago. There are in Canada, according to the last statistics published in May, 824,000 Canadians out of work, something like 116,000 more than one year ago-and this despite the substantial numbers of people who have dropped out of the labour force and are not even counted.
According to yesterday's newspaper, Mr. Parizeau, the Quebec minister of finance, said his government will seek a simple and elementary economic association with the rest of Canada if Quebec secedes. He told a group of economists at Fredericton that the Quebec and federal governments are like two boxers dancing round each other in the ring without striking any blow. He is quoted as saying, We do not know how long this circling will continue but at some point confrontation will appear and, Mr. Speaker, it will not just be politics or your political institutions that will be affected. It will also be our economy and our whole ability to carry on the economic base on which the money services of our country is set." He went on to list some of the great problems at the federal-provincial level which Ottawa causes, because of a lack of consultation. He remarked on the problem of Hydro Quebec trying to set income projections for that utility, and he noted that Ottawa's regional development policies in Quebec have left a general impression of failures. So much for the DREE efforts of Mr. Marchand, who boasted of the many millions of dollars his department had put into areas around his riding.
Then there are the pronouncements of senior civil servants who are getting into the act on what is good for the country. We find Mr. Johnson of the CBC stating that only massive expenditures through the CBC can keep the country together. He wants to make it the principal cultural force in the battle for Canadianism. He is quoted as saying: "I am going to be as fighting, aggressive, bold, loud and as honestly nationalistic as I am capable of being." But his main contentions, if followed,

June 16, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
would mean an enormous increase in the amount of money that the taxpayers spend on their CBC. If anything can be called a failure in Canadian institutions, surely it is the CBC. Are we going to follow this route and further enormously expand a government body that is obviously a failure?
Senior civil servants also seem to be getting into the act in an unprecedented way. Mr. Gordon Robertson, in a memorable speech in Halifax on Canadian unity, has been fashioning a hair shirt for the Anglophones in this country and accusing them of being the cause of Canadian disunity, and Mr. Shoya-ma has taken to the public media to denounce politicians in Alberta and Quebec for speaking out on the oil issue. These are statements from powerful civil servants such as we have never heard before in our country.
Now for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). I do feel a little sorry for him. Mr. McGillivray, writing in the Gazette of June 3, said that if the minister quits this year he will have made less of a mark on Canadian fiscal history than any other finance minister since Mr. Nowlan, who didn't even have time to present a budget. Why has he been destined to get a footnote instead of a chapter in the history of Canada? Well, he has had his problems. There is a mood of public pessimism and a loss of confidence in the government. There is a demand for restraint in government spending and we are faced with a huge budget deficit. With unemployment at about 8 per cent and with a huge balance of payments deficit the minister does have his problems. But he seems to have been only a caretaker finance minister, a reluctant dragon acting as a temporary incumbent who has not had the time or opportunity to launch new policies or initiate new strategies. Certainly his role has seemed to be to defend policies rather than make them.
The wage and price controls program has been the policy of the Prime Minister yet it is for this that the time spent by the minister in the finance department will be remembered. It was the Prime Minister who said that controls should stay on until the next election, and the minister stated he was just a simple soldier, implying that he took orders rather than gave them. When the minister goes this year his successor will inherit a $7.2 billion budget deficit, a dismal combination of high unemployment, high inflation, and a bureaucracy which has run out of ideas. It is obvious there are severe constraints on the government's ability to manage the economy and that it is time for changes and for bold action.
And what about the record of inflation? The primary cause of a reduction in inflation has been the reduction in the price of food at the farm gate brought about by bountiful harvests and a readjustment of the commodities markets around the world. The government can take no credit for this and, furthermore, prices of imported goods receded.
There is growing up a widespread feeling that anti-inflation measures tend to favour one group over another. The idea that some can receive much more than others does not sit well with the public. The fact is that more capital investment is leaving Canada than is entering after decades the other way around. Wage and price controls can only be a short term thing, supplementary at best. John K. Galbraith, for example, makes

it clear that an income and price policy does not replace a monetary and fiscal policy. He states:
It supplements it in that part of the modern economy where market control of prices and incomes has given way to private administration and where restraint on aggregate demand brings not lower prices but brings unemployment.
Our own Simon Reisman has stated:
Controls can provide time in which to re-establish sound monetary and fiscal policies. They establish a political framework in which governments can constrain wage pressures from their own large and growing public service unions.
Milton Friedman states:
There is no problem about how to stop inflation. We know how to do it. Every economist knows how to do it. I can specify it very simply. The only way to cure inflation is for the government to spend less and print less. The only way to cure inflation is to hold down the growth in the quantity of money. There is no other way to do it. There is no other device which will enable us to slow down inflation. The problem, however, is not how to stop inflation. The problem is to have the political will to do so.
We are faced with a sluggish economy. We are faced with the fact that we can become addicted to controls and use them as a convenient crutch, as an excuse in handling tough business decisions. We have become uncompetitive in world markets in fields in which we have traditionally been effective participants. A continuing control program can only heighten ineffi-cencies and make them even less competitive.
It is now agreed by all, even by those who support controls, that in the long run the retention of controls will seriously reduce the investment necessary to produce the new jobs down the road.
The stock market has not responded to the budget as it should have done, partly because profit margins are being contained by the AIB investment rules. There are many disadvantages to the AIB operations. It has to use rollback power. It has to give the impression that it is controlling wages. But it is very difficult to be fair in all aspects. The long Thompson dispute showed the difficulty of equating increases in wages in the historic wage pattern enjoyed by workers in Thompson as compared to those in Sudbury. The longer the anti-inflation controls remain, the more distorted our economy will become. Mr. Earle McLaughlin, ex president of the Royal Bank of Canada, said in January: "Let the government declare the war won and jettison the entire AIB apparatus, and, the sooner the better."
There is little convincing evidence that prices and costs are very much different now than they would have been in the absence of the control program. Government policy may have helped to sustain economic activity in Canada during the past two or three years but the United States far outpaced Canadian growth in 1976 and probably will have a considerably better economic performance this year. The United States does not have a control program at this time but the recession was much more effective in reducing inflationary expectations than was Canada's anti-inflation program. Consumer prices, including food, rose in 1976 by 9.5 per cent in Canada compared with 6.6 per cent in the United States. Wage settlements rose by about half of the Canadian increases in the past four years. So there is -grave doubt as to whether the action of the
June 16, 1977

government has materially helped to reduce inflation in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it was our party only which voted against the government on third reading of both Bill C-73 and Bill C-89 and I am happy it has taken advantage of the procedure which provides for this motion to be debated. There has been a significant deterioration in the inflation picture. The consumer price index is rising at a higher rate now than at Christmas, and other price indices show that controls no longer contain inflation. Mr. Turner, the previous finance minister, announced that there was a restraint program in effect since June of 1975, but the main federal spending estimates have increased by 28 per cent. Since that time the narrow measures of money supply increased by 16 per cent while wider measures record increases of 31 per cent; that is Ml and M2. Controls no longer work, and federal restraint is non-existent.
If the federal government and the provincial governments control the money supply in a reasonable way, increases in the public sector will be dampened by the high degree of slack in the economy. This should result in a slowing of wage and price demands and accordingly a lower risk of a renewed wage and price problem. Certainly we need business recovery and business investment, and to ensure this the administration must adopt a proper fiscal stance. There is no doubt about it that the AIB must be regarded as of importance in assessing one's business decisions.
As a professional myself who has had to report to the Anti-Inflation Board, I can vouch for the complexity of the forms that have to be filled out to meet even minimum compliance. They were so complicated I could not even begin to fill them out. It cost $1,000 to fill them out to comply with the so-called protected category. The professionals and selfemployed have a so-called ceiling of $2,400 which may be exceeded if there is more productivity-again something very difficult to prove but one which annoys very hard working people who find themselves held to a much smaller rate of increase. This ceiling has created a great deal of unhappiness and a feeling of frustration among working people.
My colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), has put forward suggestions by which our party might establish a reasonable decontrol program and which would, I think, be an improvement on what the green paper has suggested. The Prime Minister has mentioned the need for business and labour to meet and to reach decisions that will decrease the inflation process and deal with price problems. But this consultation process should be much larger than just large labour and large business. It must include consumers and producers and more junior governments, both provincial and municipal. I will not dwell on these suggestions which I think bear merit and might well be incorporated into government measures. But, Mr. Speaker, all will come to naught unless the governments make fundamental changes as compared to what they have done in the past.
Anti-Inflation Act
Someone has said that since the era of Alexander the Great wars always created inflation. The one thing they have in common is massive intervention in the economy by the government. Up until recent years, inflation occurred in western nations whenever wars existed and it was necessary for governments to take into the economy many hundreds of thousands of soldiers and those who worked in the munitions factories, whether they made guns or swords.
But in recent years in western democracy there has grown up a new phenomenon-the massive transfer of funds to government agencies for our many welfare and socially oriented programs. These programs are obviously very acceptable and do a great deal to alleviate harsh social conditions, but they also seem, when carried to extreme, to be a potent factor for increasing the inflation rate in the economy. The last ten years have seen a massive increase in these social programs as they rush toward maturity. It is probably safe to say that many of these programs were not seen to be expensive when they were put into effect. Introduction of the old age pension and Canada pension along with the rapid increase in inflation made the value of savings extremely doubtful, at least for bonds, trusts, and the usual form of savings instruments.
The government has just recently brought into the House a measure to tax savings in insurance companies. Although the tax may not be retroactive, it already shows how government action can interfere with the long term plans of the individual and erase much of the savings that he might have expected to accrue. On strictly ethical grounds it probably can be justified but it makes reliance on long term savings more doubtful. It becomes obvious to the individual that he cannot plan ahead. If he does, almost certainly the government will change the rules of the game and he will find he is quite severely penalized. The inflation rate increases the doubtful value of savings and hence makes us a consumer group of citizens- better to take a foreign trip than to save money which steadily loses its value. This probably is one of the reasons why our foreign trade deficit in tourism is so high. Therefore the percentage of the GNP which the government takes must be carefully regulated. Obviously, if it takes too much, productivity will decrease because the worker will work less and less.
Recent figures indicate that the government's share of the GNP may have stabilized. It is to be hoped that this is so. I think one of the most important weapons in the fight against inflation is that governments not take more than they have from the GNP. Otherwise we will be in trouble.
There are a good many obvious causes of inflation, but the prime one is government policy and government practices, either directly by spending, borrowing or control of the money supply. There are also myriad government rules on business operations and the cost of complying, as well as indirectly by nudging up pay scales, such as minimum wages, and finally if wages rise faster than the value of goods and services produced.
While I have said that in the past wars took most of our money, today our welfare and social programs are taking up the slack. We are enjoying many of the things we have

The most important factor in controlling inflation is obviously control of government expenditure, and it must be controlled at a reasonable rate or the GNP will be exceeded and inflation will result.
